Italian menu words.Antipasti: Literally 'before the meal', this first course often features cured meats, cheeses and marinated vegetables.
Italian menu words.Primi: The first course, usually pasta, risotto or soup, is the heart of an Italian meal and comes before the meat or fish.
Italian menu words.Secondi: The 'second' course is the main meat or fish dish, and it's typically served without a side.
Italian menu words.Contorni: Sides such as greens or roast potatoes are ordered separately, since Italian main courses usually arrive without them.
Italian menu words.Dolci: The sweets course, which can include tiramisu, panna cotta or gelato, closes a meal before coffee.
Italian menu words.Al forno: Means 'from the oven', and flags dishes baked such as lasagne or roasted potatoes.
Italian menu words.Alla griglia: Italian for grilled, as in pesce alla griglia, a way of cooking over an open flame.
Italian menu words.Fritto misto: A 'mixed fry' of battered seafood or vegetables, crisp from hot oil, a coastal classic.
Italian menu words.Della casa: 'Of the house' marks the restaurant's own wine or specialty, often a good-value choice.
Italian menu words.Crudo: Means 'raw', a plate of thinly sliced raw fish or meat dressed with olive oil and lemon, similar to sashimi.
Italian menu words.Al dente: 'To the tooth': pasta cooked so it still has a slight bite in the center, which Italians insist upon.
Italian menu words.Bistecca: Italian for steak, with the famed bistecca alla fiorentina being a huge T-bone grilled rare over coals in Tuscany.
Italian menu words.Digestivo: A bitter or herbal after-dinner liqueur, like amaro or grappa, sipped to settle a heavy meal.
Italian menu words.Entrée: A trap: this French word means starter in France, but in the US it means the main course, and it isn't Italian.
Italian menu words.Hors d'oeuvre: French for 'outside the work', meaning a small bite before the meal, it isn't an Italian term.
Italian menu words.Amuse-bouche: Chefs send out this bite-size freebie to 'amuse the mouth'; it's French.
Italian menu words.À la carte: French for 'by the menu', where each dish is priced separately, not Italian.
Italian menu words.Tapas: Small Spanish plates, said to come from the custom of covering a drink with a slice of bread; not Italian.
Italian menu words.Mezze: A spread of small dishes across the Middle East and Eastern Mediterranean.
Italian menu words.Prix fixe: French for 'fixed price', a multi-course meal at one price, so it's not Italian.
Italian menu words.Plat du jour: French for 'dish of the day', the chef's daily special.
Italian menu words.Au jus: French for 'with juice', describing meat served with its own natural juices, as in a French dip sandwich.
Italian menu words.Bon appétit: French for 'good appetite', said before eating; Italians say buon appetito.
Italian menu words.Digestif: The French spelling of the after-dinner drink; the Italian version is digestivo, so the 'f' gives it away.

Landlocked countries in Europe.Hungary: Landlocked at the heart of the Carpathian Basin. Lake Balaton, central Europe's largest lake, is its 'Hungarian sea'.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Czech Republic: Landlocked, but Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale famously gives 'Bohemia' a seacoast, which the real Bohemia never had.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Slovakia: Landlocked, and the Danube forms part of its southern border. Its capital, Bratislava, sits near both Austria and Hungary.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Serbia: Serbia became landlocked in 2006 when Montenegro declared independence. The Danube and Sava rivers meet at Belgrade.
Landlocked countries in Europe.North Macedonia: A Balkan country with Lake Ohrid, one of Europe's oldest and deepest lakes, but no sea coast.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Liechtenstein: A tiny Alpine principality. It's doubly landlocked, meaning every neighbor, Switzerland and Austria, is itself landlocked.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Luxembourg: A small, wealthy country with no coast, one of the world's few grand duchies. It holds the EU's top court.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Andorra: A Pyrenees principality between France and Spain, and it has two co-princes, one of whom is France's president.
Landlocked countries in Europe.San Marino: One of the world's oldest republics, said to date to 301 CE, entirely surrounded by Italy and on the slopes of Monte Titano.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Belarus: Landlocked in Eastern Europe, and its Białowieża Forest holds Europe's largest population of wild bison.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Moldova: A landlocked country known for the world's largest wine cellar, Mileștii Mici, with underground tunnels stretching on for kilometers.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Slovenia: Slovenia isn't landlocked. It has a short Adriatic coast of about 47 kilometers, near the port of Koper.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Croatia: Croatia has one of the Mediterranean's most indented coastlines, with over a thousand islands.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Belgium: Belgium has a short North Sea coast, about 65 kilometers, popular with Belgians for the tram that runs along it.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Netherlands: A North Sea country, and much of its land lies at or below sea level, protected by dikes.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Denmark: Denmark is a peninsula plus over 400 islands, so nowhere there is more than about 50 kilometers from the sea.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Montenegro: It has an Adriatic coast, including the Bay of Kotor, so it's not landlocked, and it left Serbia landlocked in 2006.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Albania: Albania has coasts on both the Adriatic and the Ionian seas, so it is not landlocked.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Bosnia: Bosnia and Herzegovina has a tiny coastal strip of about 20 kilometers at Neum, which makes it nearly landlocked but not quite.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Romania: Romania has a Black Sea coast, and the Danube ends in its delta, which is a UNESCO site.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Bulgaria: Bulgaria has a Black Sea coast with popular resorts, so it is not landlocked.
Landlocked countries in Europe.Monaco: A trap, since Monaco is tiny but borders the Mediterranean, so it is not landlocked.

Animals with horns (not antlers).Llama: Llamas are camelids with no horns or antlers at all, though they sometimes spit when annoyed.

Flowers.Rose: Roses have been cultivated for thousands of years, and there are over 150 species and tens of thousands of cultivars.
Flowers.Tulip: Tulips caused 'tulip mania' in 1630s Holland, when single bulbs sold for more than the price of a house.
Flowers.Daisy: A daisy's 'flower' is really a head of many tiny flowers, and its name comes from 'day's eye' because it opens at dawn.
Flowers.Lily: Lilies are grown from bulbs, and some, like the Easter lily, are symbols of spring, but many are toxic to cats.
Flowers.Orchid: Orchids are one of the largest plant families, with tens of thousands of species, and vanilla is the fruit of an orchid.
Flowers.Sunflower: Sunflowers are not one flower but hundreds, and young heads turn to follow the sun across the sky.
Flowers.Daffodil: Daffodils are Wales's national flower and a sign of spring, and all parts of the plant are poisonous.
Flowers.Peony: Peonies can live for decades, even a century, and in China they've been called the king of flowers.
Flowers.Carnation: Carnations have been grown for over 2,000 years and are a Mother's Day flower in many countries.
Flowers.Marigold: Marigolds are edible and bright orange, and their petals were once used to color butter and cheese.
Flowers.Iris: Iris is named after the Greek goddess of the rainbow, and the fleur-de-lis emblem is a stylized iris.
Flowers.Poppy: Poppies are the symbol of remembrance because they bloomed on First World War battlefields, and opium comes from one species.
Flowers.Dahlia: Dahlias came from Mexico, where they're the national flower, and their tubers were once eaten by the Aztecs.
Flowers.Lavender: Lavender is a flowering plant in the mint family, famed for its scent, and its name comes from the Latin for 'to wash'.
Flowers.Fern: Ferns never produce flowers; they reproduce by spores, and that's why they don't belong here.
Flowers.Moss: Moss has no flowers, and these tiny plants reproduce by spores, living in damp, shady spots.
Flowers.Ivy: Ivy is a clinging evergreen vine that blooms only once mature, so it's grown for its leaves rather than flowers.
Flowers.Basil: Basil is grown for its leaves, and while its flowers are edible, gardeners pinch them off to keep the leaves tasty.
Flowers.Bamboo: Bamboo is a grass, and it flowers only rarely, some species just once in 60 to 120 years.
Flowers.Kelp: Kelp is a marine algae, so it never produces flowers, and its forests are among the fastest growing organisms.
Flowers.Pine: Pine trees reproduce with cones rather than flowers, which makes them conifers, not flowering plants.
Flowers.Mushroom: Mushrooms are fungi, not plants, and they produce spores instead of flowers.
Flowers.Spinach: Spinach is a leafy vegetable that bolts into flower in warm weather, but nobody grows it for the blooms.
Flowers.Lichen: Lichen is a partnership between a fungus and algae, so it isn't a plant and never flowers.

French sauces.Béchamel: Béchamel, milk thickened with a white roux, is one of the five French mother sauces, and it's the base of mac and cheese and lasagne.
French sauces.Hollandaise: Hollandaise is a warm emulsion of egg yolk, butter and lemon, and it's another mother sauce that curdles if overheated.
French sauces.Béarnaise: Béarnaise is hollandaise with tarragon and shallots, and its name refers to Béarn, a region in southwest France.
French sauces.Velouté: Velouté is a stock-based mother sauce thickened with roux, and its name means 'velvety'.
French sauces.Espagnole: Espagnole is the rich brown mother sauce, made from browned roux and stock, and the base of demi-glace.
French sauces.Beurre blanc: Beurre blanc is a 'white butter' sauce from the Loire valley, whipped with shallots and vinegar into a creamy emulsion.
French sauces.Mornay: Mornay is a béchamel enriched with cheese, usually Gruyère, and it's the sauce behind many gratins.
French sauces.Rémoulade: Rémoulade is a mayonnaise-based sauce with pickles, capers and herbs, and it's often served with fried fish.
French sauces.Bordelaise: Bordelaise is a red wine sauce from Bordeaux, often with bone marrow and shallots, and goes with steak.
French sauces.Mayonnaise: Mayonnaise is a cold emulsion of egg yolk and oil, and it's thought to be named after Mahón in Minorca after a French victory in 1756.
French sauces.Ravigote: Ravigote is a tangy sauce of herbs, capers and vinegar, and its name means 'to invigorate'.
French sauces.Pesto: Pesto is Italian, from Genoa, so it's not one of the French sauces.
French sauces.Marinara: Marinara is an Italian tomato sauce, so it's not French.
French sauces.Chimichurri: Chimichurri is an Argentine sauce, not French, and its origin is unclear.
French sauces.Tzatziki: Tzatziki is Greek, a yogurt-cucumber dip, not a French sauce.
French sauces.Romesco: Romesco is a Spanish sauce from Catalonia of roasted peppers and nuts, and it's not French.
French sauces.Sriracha: Sriracha is a Thai chili sauce, so it isn't a French sauce.
French sauces.Teriyaki: Teriyaki is Japanese, a sweet soy glaze, and not French.
French sauces.Mole: Mole is Mexican, with a long list of chilies and spices, so it's not French.
French sauces.Harissa: Harissa is a North African chili paste, so it isn't a French sauce, although it's popular in France.
French sauces.Worcestershire: Worcestershire sauce is English, made with fermented anchovies and tamarind, and it's not French.
French sauces.Ketchup: Ketchup is of Asian origin, from a fermented fish sauce, so it isn't a French sauce.
French sauces.Hoisin: Hoisin is Chinese, so it's not one of the French sauces.
French sauces.Ponzu: Ponzu is a Japanese citrus soy sauce, and not French.

Beer styles.IPA: Short for India Pale Ale. The hoppy style was reputedly brewed with extra hops to survive the long sea voyage from England to India.
Beer styles.Stout: Dark, roasted beer, whose name came from a 'stout porter'. Guinness is the world's best-known; its famous nitrogen head gives a creamy pour.
Beer styles.Porter: A dark London beer of the 1700s, named for the street and river porters who drank it. Stout began as a stronger porter.
Beer styles.Lager: From the German for 'to store', a beer fermented cold and aged for weeks. Most of the world's beer is lager.
Beer styles.Pilsner: Born in 1842 in Plzeň, in today's Czech Republic, the first golden lager. It remains the world's most-copied beer style.
Beer styles.Hefeweizen: German wheat beer, whose name means 'yeast wheat'. Its banana and clove flavours come from the yeast itself, not added fruit.
Beer styles.Saison: A Belgian farmhouse ale, once brewed in winter to refresh farm workers in summer. Its name is French for season.
Beer styles.Bock: Strong German lager, whose name is the goat in the German, so many bottles carry a goat on the label. It's from Einbeck.
Beer styles.Pale ale: The traditional English style, brewed with top-fermenting yeast. Its name came from the pale malt used, compared with dark beers.
Beer styles.Kölsch: Cologne's local beer, an ale fermented warm but conditioned cold. Only brewers in Cologne can legally use the name.
Beer styles.Dunkel: German for 'dark', a malty Bavarian lager the colour of bread crust. It's the old Munich style, from before the invention of golden lagers.
Beer styles.Lambic: A Belgian beer fermented spontaneously by wild yeasts floating in the air near Brussels. It's sour, and the base of gueuze and fruit kriek.
Beer styles.Cider: A trap: cider is fermented apple juice, not brewed from grain. It's a separate drink from beer.
Beer styles.Mead: Honey wine, one of the oldest alcoholic drinks in the world, not made from grain. Not beer.
Beer styles.Sake: Japanese rice wine, which is often called rice beer but is brewed with a process that converts starch and ferments at the same time. Not beer.
Beer styles.Perry: A trap: fermented pear juice, the pear cousin of cider. It is made from fruit, not from malted grain, so it is not a beer style.
Beer styles.Kombucha: A trap: fermented sweet tea made with a bacteria-yeast culture. It is fizzy, but it uses no grain, so it is not a beer style.
Beer styles.Merlot: A trap: a red grape variety and the wine made from it. Wine comes from grapes, not malted grain, so it is not a beer style.
Beer styles.Prosecco: A trap: Italy's sparkling wine, made from Glera grapes. It has bubbles like beer, but it is grape wine and not beer.
Beer styles.Sherry: A trap: a fortified wine from Spain's Jerez region, aged in a special solera system. It is wine, not a beer style.
Beer styles.Port: A trap: a sweet fortified wine from Portugal's Douro Valley, named after the city of Porto. It is wine, not a beer style.
Beer styles.Grappa: A clear Italian brandy, distilled from the leftover grape skins and seeds after wine pressing. A spirit, not a beer.
Beer styles.Soju: Korea's clear spirit, traditionally from rice and now often from other starches. It is a spirit, not beer.
Beer styles.Vermouth: A fortified wine flavoured with botanicals, essential for martinis and Manhattans. Not beer.

Mountain ranges in Asia.Karakoram: Includes K2 and some of the longest glaciers outside the polar regions. Its name is Turkic for 'black gravel'.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Hindu Kush: A range stretching across Afghanistan and Pakistan, where Alexander the Great's army crossed. Its name may mean 'Killer of Hindus', from the slave trade.

Mountain ranges in Asia.Tian Shan: The 'Celestial Mountains' of Central Asia, running through Kyrgyzstan and Xinjiang. Their name is Chinese, and Silk Road caravans crossed them.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Zagros: A range running through Iran and Iraq, whose slopes are home to ancient farming. Oil lies beneath the foothills.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Kunlun: A Chinese range along the northern edge of Tibet, in Chinese mythology the home of the Queen Mother of the West.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Pamirs: Called the 'Roof of the World', this Central Asian knot is where the Himalaya, Karakoram, Kunlun, and Hindu Kush meet.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Taurus: A range in southern Turkey above the Mediterranean, from which Noah's tales. Its name is thought to come from a Greek word for bull.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Alps: A trap: Europe's great mountain chain, spanning eight countries, from France to Slovenia. Not in Asia.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Andes: A trap: the world's longest continental range, at about 7,000 km down South America. Not Asian.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Rockies: A trap: North America's range, stretching from Canada to New Mexico. It is not in Asia.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Pyrenees: A trap: the range between France and Spain, with tiny Andorra tucked inside. It is not Asian.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Atlas: A North African range running through Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia. It is named for the Titan Atlas of Greek myth.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Appalachians: An eastern North American range, old and worn, far older than the Rockies. The Appalachian Trail runs along it.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Carpathians: A curved range through Central and Eastern Europe, home to Transylvania and the Dracula legend. European.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Apennines: A trap: the backbone of Italy, running down the peninsula's whole length. It is European, not Asian.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Dolomites: A trap: Italy's pale limestone peaks, a UNESCO World Heritage site. They are European, not Asian.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Drakensberg: A trap: South Africa's highest range, whose name is Afrikaans for 'Dragon Mountains'. It is African, not Asian.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Cascades: A volcanic range from British Columbia to northern California, including Mount St. Helens. American.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Balkans: A trap: the mountains that give the Balkan Peninsula its name, in southeastern Europe. Not Asian.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Sierra Nevada: Spain's Sierra Nevada is home to its highest peak on the mainland; California's range includes Yosemite. Not Asian.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Great Dividing Range: A trap: Australia's longest range, running down the east coast for about 3,500 km. It is not in Asia.
Mountain ranges in Asia.Dinaric Alps: A Balkan range along the Adriatic coast, in Croatia and Bosnia, of limestone karst. European.

Countries whose currency is a dollar.Guyana: Guyana's dollar is the currency of the only English-speaking country in South America.
Countries whose currency is a dollar.Barbados: The Barbadian dollar has been pegged at two to one against the US dollar for decades.

Countries whose currency is a dollar.Mexico: Mexico's currency is the peso, and the dollar sign $ actually came from the Spanish peso, before the US dollar.

Countries whose currency is a dollar.South Africa: South Africa's rand is named for the Witwatersrand, the gold-bearing ridge near Johannesburg.

Countries whose currency is a dollar.Malaysia: The ringgit, Malaysia's currency, means jagged, after the serrated edges of old Spanish silver coins.
Countries whose currency is a dollar.Ireland: Ireland uses the euro, having given up the Irish pound in 2002.
Countries whose currency is a dollar.Egypt: Egypt's currency is the Egyptian pound, one of the oldest in the Middle East.
Countries whose currency is a dollar.Chile: Chile uses the peso, and as in Mexico, the $ sign is used for it.

Words for bodies of water.Lagoon: A shallow body of water cut off from the open sea by sandbars or reefs, as in Venice, whose famous city sits in one.
Words for bodies of water.Estuary: Where a river meets the sea and fresh water mixes with salt, creating rich wildlife habitat, as in the Thames or Chesapeake Bay.
Words for bodies of water.Strait: A narrow channel joining two seas. The Strait of Gibraltar is only about 14 km wide and separates Europe from Africa.
Words for bodies of water.Bay: A curve of coastline where the sea reaches inland. The Bay of Bengal is the largest in the world, at about 2.2 million square km.
Words for bodies of water.Gulf: A large bay with a narrower mouth. The Gulf of Mexico is the largest gulf in the world, about 1.6 million square km.
Words for bodies of water.Sound: It can be a long sea inlet or channel, as in Puget Sound, so it sneaks in as water, not only a noise.
Words for bodies of water.Inlet: A narrow arm of water that pushes into land from the sea or a lake, often drowned river valleys or glacier-carved fjords.
Words for bodies of water.Loch: The Scottish word for a lake or sea inlet. Loch Ness holds more fresh water than all the lakes of England and Wales combined.
Words for bodies of water.Tarn: A small mountain lake in a hollow carved by a glacier, a word common in the Lake District of northern England.
Words for bodies of water.Bayou: A slow, marshy waterway of the American South, likely from the Choctaw word bayuk, meaning small stream, as in Louisiana.
Words for bodies of water.Creek: A small stream in North America, but in Britain and Australia a creek can be a narrow tidal inlet from the sea.
Words for bodies of water.Pond: A small body of still water, usually shallow enough for sunlight to reach the bottom and let plants take root.
Words for bodies of water.Reservoir: An artificial lake that stores water. Lake Mead, created by the Hoover Dam, is the largest reservoir in the United States.
Words for bodies of water.Cape: A headland jutting into the sea is land, not water, like Cape Horn at the tip of South America.
Words for bodies of water.Ridge: A long narrow strip of high ground, which is land, even though it can divide river basins.
Words for bodies of water.Cliff: A steep rock face is a land feature, though it often drops straight into the sea.
Words for bodies of water.Moor: Open, uncultivated upland, often boggy, but it is land and not water, as on Dartmoor or Exmoor.
Words for bodies of water.Knoll: A small rounded hill, famously the grassy knoll in Dallas, and land rather than water.
Words for bodies of water.Bluff: A steep headland or cliff that often overlooks water but is itself land, as on the Mississippi.
Words for bodies of water.Glen: A narrow valley, especially in Scotland and Ireland, and land even when a stream runs along it.
Words for bodies of water.Steppe: A vast treeless grassland, like the one that stretches across Central Asia, and not water.
Words for bodies of water.Savanna: Tropical grassland with scattered trees, such as the Serengeti, so land, not water.
Words for bodies of water.Hill: A raised landform lower than a mountain, so not water, though many rivers rise on hills.
Words for bodies of water.Mesa: A flat-topped rocky landform with steep sides, whose name means table in Spanish, so land, not water.

Correct US state capitals.Texas: Austin: Austin is famed for live music and for the largest urban bat colony in North America, under the Congress Avenue Bridge.
Correct US state capitals.Ohio: Columbus: Columbus is named for Christopher Columbus and is now Ohio's largest city as well as its capital.
Correct US state capitals.Nevada: Carson City: Carson City was named for frontiersman Kit Carson and boomed with the nearby Comstock silver strike.
Correct US state capitals.Oregon: Salem: Salem's name is thought to come from the Hebrew word for peace, and it sits in the Willamette Valley.
Correct US state capitals.Florida: Tallahassee: Tallahassee was picked in 1824 as a midpoint between the old Spanish towns of St. Augustine and Pensacola.
Correct US state capitals.Alaska: Juneau: Juneau is the only US state capital that can't be reached by road; you arrive by boat or plane.
Correct US state capitals.Kansas: Topeka: Topeka was the home of the Brown v. Board of Education case, and its name is often said to mean 'a good place to dig potatoes'.
Correct US state capitals.Maine: Augusta: Augusta lies on the Kennebec River and is one of the smaller state capitals, much smaller than Portland.
Correct US state capitals.Iowa: Des Moines: Des Moines has a Capitol dome covered in gold leaf, and Iowa's biggest city is also its capital.
Correct US state capitals.Idaho: Boise: Boise's name is often traced to French trappers calling the tree-lined river 'boisé', meaning wooded, in a dry landscape.
Correct US state capitals.Utah: Salt Lake City: Salt Lake City was founded in 1847 by Mormon pioneers led by Brigham Young.
Correct US state capitals.Vermont: Montpelier: Montpelier is the smallest state capital by population, and the only one without a McDonald's.
Correct US state capitals.Texas: Houston: Houston is Texas's largest city and named for Sam Houston, but the capital is Austin.
Correct US state capitals.Ohio: Cleveland: Cleveland hosts the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame but isn't Ohio's capital; Columbus is.
Correct US state capitals.Nevada: Las Vegas: Las Vegas is Nevada's biggest city by far, but the capital is Carson City.
Correct US state capitals.Oregon: Portland: Portland is Oregon's largest city, but the capital is Salem.
Correct US state capitals.Florida: Miami: Miami is Florida's famous coastal city, but the capital is Tallahassee, far to the north.
Correct US state capitals.Alaska: Anchorage: Anchorage holds about 40 percent of Alaska's people, but the capital is Juneau.
Correct US state capitals.Kansas: Wichita: Wichita is Kansas's largest city, but the capital is Topeka.
Correct US state capitals.Maine: Portland: There's another Portland, in Maine, and it's the state's largest city; Augusta is the capital.
Correct US state capitals.Kentucky: Louisville: Louisville is Kentucky's largest city and home of the Kentucky Derby, but the capital is Frankfort.
Correct US state capitals.Illinois: Chicago: Chicago towers over Illinois, but the capital is Springfield, once Abraham Lincoln's home.
Correct US state capitals.Michigan: Detroit: Detroit is the Motor City, but Michigan's capital is Lansing.
Correct US state capitals.Georgia: Savannah: Savannah was Georgia's first capital and is full of historic squares, but today the capital is Atlanta.

Constellations of the zodiac.Aries: Aries is the ram, and thanks to precession the March equinox no longer sits in it but in Pisces.
Constellations of the zodiac.Taurus: Taurus holds the Pleiades and the Hyades star clusters, and Aldebaran is the bull's red eye.
Constellations of the zodiac.Gemini: Gemini is named for the twins Castor and Pollux, and the Geminids each December are among the best meteor showers.
Constellations of the zodiac.Cancer: Cancer is the faintest zodiac constellation, but it holds the Beehive Cluster, visible to the naked eye.
Constellations of the zodiac.Leo: Leo is led by Regulus, and the Leonids meteors seem to radiate from it each November.
Constellations of the zodiac.Virgo: Virgo is the largest zodiac constellation, second-largest of all 88, with the bright star Spica.
Constellations of the zodiac.Libra: Libra is the only zodiac sign that is an object, and it was once seen as the scorpion's claws.
Constellations of the zodiac.Scorpius: Scorpius has Antares, a red supergiant, as the scorpion's heart.
Constellations of the zodiac.Sagittarius: Sagittarius is where our view points toward the Milky Way's center, with a black hole there.
Constellations of the zodiac.Capricornus: Capricornus is a sea-goat, a half goat, half fish creature that goes back to ancient Babylon.
Constellations of the zodiac.Aquarius: Aquarius is the water-bearer, and the Eta Aquariids meteor shower comes from Halley's Comet debris.
Constellations of the zodiac.Pisces: Pisces shows two fish tied together, and the Sun now crosses the March equinox there.
Constellations of the zodiac.Orion: Orion is famous but isn't zodiacal; the Sun's path does not pass through it.
Constellations of the zodiac.Cassiopeia: Cassiopeia's W shape is easy to spot but lies far from the Sun's path.
Constellations of the zodiac.Andromeda: Andromeda is named for a princess in Greek myth, and it's not on the zodiac.
Constellations of the zodiac.Pegasus: Pegasus is the winged horse, and its Great Square is a well-known sight, but it's not a zodiac constellation.
Constellations of the zodiac.Ursa Major: Ursa Major, the Great Bear, is circumpolar in the north, far from the zodiac belt.
Constellations of the zodiac.Cygnus: Cygnus is the swan with the Northern Cross and isn't on the Sun's path.
Constellations of the zodiac.Draco: Draco is a long dragon wrapped around the north pole, not in the zodiac.
Constellations of the zodiac.Lyra: Lyra is small but holds bright Vega, and it's not in the zodiac.
Constellations of the zodiac.Perseus: Perseus is a hero of Greek myth with the Perseids meteor shower, not part of the zodiac.
Constellations of the zodiac.Hercules: Hercules is a huge constellation but is not part of the zodiac.
Constellations of the zodiac.Centaurus: Centaurus is southern and holds Alpha Centauri, so it's not in the zodiac.
Constellations of the zodiac.Cepheus: Cepheus is a king in Greek myth in the north sky, outside the zodiac.

Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Tyrannosaurus rex: Its bite force was perhaps the strongest of any land animal ever, around 35,000 newtons, enough to crush bone. It lived about 68 million years ago.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Triceratops: Its name means three-horned face. Its huge frill and horns may have been used for display, and it was among the last dinosaurs alive.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Stegosaurus: Plated back and spiked tail, but a brain about the size of a lime or small apple. It lived about 150 million years ago.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Velociraptor: In reality it was turkey-sized and covered in feathers, far smaller than in Jurassic Park. It lived in what is now Mongolia.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Brachiosaurus: A giraffe-like sauropod with front legs longer than its back legs. It weighed perhaps 30 to 50 tons.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Diplodocus: A very long, slender sauropod up to about 25 meters. Much of that length was its whip-like tail.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Spinosaurus: The largest predatory dinosaur known, with a sail on its back. It hunted fish and was likely semi-aquatic.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Ankylosaurus: An armored tank with a bony tail club that could break bones. Even its eyelids were armored.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Iguanodon: One of the first dinosaurs ever named, in 1825. It had a thumb spike, and it was long misdrawn with the spike on its nose.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Allosaurus: The top predator of Late Jurassic North America, which preceded T. rex by about 80 million years.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Parasaurolophus: A duck-billed dinosaur with a long curved head crest. The hollow crest likely worked as a trumpet for calls.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Pterodactyl: A trap: pterosaurs were flying reptiles, relatives of dinosaurs but not dinosaurs themselves. The popular name loosely refers to Pterodactylus.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Plesiosaur: A trap: a marine reptile with a long neck, not a dinosaur. Its ancient discovery by Mary Anning in 1823 stunned scientists.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Mosasaur: A trap: a giant ocean lizard-like reptile, related to monitor lizards and snakes, not a dinosaur.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Ichthyosaur: A trap: a dolphin-shaped marine reptile that gave live birth in the sea, not a dinosaur.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Dimetrodon: A trap: sail-backed, but it's more closely related to mammals than dinosaurs, and lived before dinosaurs appeared.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Woolly mammoth: A trap: an Ice Age mammal, tens of millions of years after the last dinosaurs. Some survived until about 4,000 years ago.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Saber-toothed cat: A trap: a mammal of the Ice Age, appearing tens of millions of years after the dinosaurs died out.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Megalodon: A trap: a giant shark, a fish, not a dinosaur. It lived about 23 to 3.6 million years ago.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Dodo: A trap: a flightless bird, which is technically a dinosaur descendant, but it is not itself called a dinosaur. It died out in the 1600s.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Komodo dragon: A trap: the largest living lizard, up to about 3 meters long, is a reptile with a dinosaur-like look, but not a dinosaur.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Mastodon: A trap: an extinct elephant relative of the Ice Age, long after the dinosaurs, and not a dinosaur itself.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Quetzalcoatlus: A trap: a giant pterosaur with a wingspan of about 10 meters. It was a flying reptile, not a dinosaur.
Dinosaurs (not just anything prehistoric.Coelacanth: A trap: a fish thought extinct with the dinosaurs until one was caught in 1938. It's not a dinosaur.

Deep-sea creatures.Anglerfish: The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure from its head to attract prey in total darkness. Tiny males fuse permanently onto females.
Deep-sea creatures.Gulper eel: The gulper eel has a huge mouth and a whip-like tail ending in a glowing tip, and it can swallow prey bigger than itself.
Deep-sea creatures.Vampire squid: The vampire squid, despite its name, feeds on drifting marine snow rather than blood, and it turns itself inside out when threatened.
Deep-sea creatures.Giant squid: Giant squid have the largest eyes in the animal kingdom, about the size of a dinner plate, and were first filmed alive only in 2004.
Deep-sea creatures.Dumbo octopus: The Dumbo octopus flaps ear-like fins to swim and lives deeper than any other known octopus, in water thousands of meters down.
Deep-sea creatures.Barreleye: The barreleye has a transparent head, with tubular eyes visible inside that rotate to look up or forward.
Deep-sea creatures.Fangtooth: The fangtooth has the largest teeth for its size of any ocean fish, so long that it has sockets in the roof of its mouth to hold them.
Deep-sea creatures.Viperfish: The viperfish has fang-like teeth so long they don't fit in the mouth, and it lights up with glowing organs along its body.
Deep-sea creatures.Giant isopod: Giant isopods look like enormous woodlice and can survive years without food, and they feed on dead creatures falling from above.
Deep-sea creatures.Blobfish: The blobfish looks sad only when pulled up. In its home depths the pressure keeps it looking like a normal fish.
Deep-sea creatures.Frilled shark: The frilled shark has 300 needle-like teeth and an eel-like body, and it is often called a living fossil.
Deep-sea creatures.Goblin shark: The goblin shark has a long flat snout and a jaw that shoots forward to snatch prey, and its skin looks pink.
Deep-sea creatures.Giant tube worm: Giant tube worms live near hydrothermal vents, with no mouth or gut. Bacteria inside them turn chemicals into food.
Deep-sea creatures.Clownfish: Clownfish live in sunlit reefs, shallow water, and are made famous by Finding Nemo, and they shelter among anemone stingers.
Deep-sea creatures.Sea otter: Sea otters live in shallow coastal waters and have the densest fur of any animal, up to a million hairs per square inch.
Deep-sea creatures.Manatee: Manatees graze in shallow, warm waters and rivers, and are related to elephants, far from the deep sea.
Deep-sea creatures.Seahorse: Seahorses live among shallow seagrass, and it is the males who carry and give birth to the young.
Deep-sea creatures.Parrotfish: Parrotfish live on shallow reefs, and they bite coral with beak-like teeth, then excrete it as fine white sand.
Deep-sea creatures.Puffin: A puffin dives only a few dozen meters at most, and it is a seabird, not a deep-sea animal.
Deep-sea creatures.Pelican: Pelicans plunge into shallow water to scoop fish, and are birds that stay near the surface.
Deep-sea creatures.Sea lion: Sea lions can dive deep, hundreds of meters, but they live in coastal waters and they are mammals, not deep-sea creatures.
Deep-sea creatures.Goldfish: Goldfish are freshwater pond fish, and they can live decades in the right conditions.
Deep-sea creatures.Beaver: Beavers live in freshwater streams and lakes, building lodges and dams, not in the deep sea.
Deep-sea creatures.Flamingo: Flamingos wade in shallow lakes and get their pink color from the pigments in the shrimp and algae they eat.

Hanna-Barbera characters.Fred Flintstone: His 'yabba dabba doo' was reportedly an ad-lib by Alan Reed that replaced the scripted 'yahoo'.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Scooby-Doo: The Great Dane's name came from the 'doo-be-doo-be-doo' scat in Frank Sinatra's song 'Strangers in the Night'.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Yogi Bear: The bear who is 'smarter than the average bear' lives in Jellystone Park and steals pic-a-nic baskets.
Hanna-Barbera characters.George Jetson: The Jetsons lived in 2062, and George's job is pushing a button, working about an hour a day, two days a week.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Huckleberry Hound: The blue, laid-back hound with a Southern drawl hosted the first cartoon series to win an Emmy, in 1960.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Top Cat: Boss Cat in Britain; the leader of a gang of alley cats, with a Sgt. Bilko-style con-man spirit.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Snagglepuss: The pink lion who says 'Exit, stage left!' was voiced by Daws Butler in the style of Bert Lahr, who played the Cowardly Lion.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Quick Draw McGraw: The horse sheriff's alter ego is El Kabong, a masked hero who swings a guitar to knock out outlaws.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Dick Dastardly: The mustached Wacky Races villain cheats constantly and never wins, and he and Muttley later chased a pigeon in their own show.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Muttley: Dick Dastardly's sidekick dog is famed for a wheezing snicker and for demanding a medal whenever his boss's scheme works.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Barney Rubble: Fred's easygoing neighbor and the father of the superstrong Bamm-Bamm, adopted by him and Betty.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Boo Boo: Yogi's small, bow-tied sidekick is the one who warns that the park ranger is coming, and he is the voice of caution.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Astro: Astro, the Jetsons' family dog, was voiced by Don Messick, who also voiced Scooby-Doo and Boo Boo Bear.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Bugs Bunny: Bugs belongs to Warner Bros., not Hanna-Barbera, although Hanna and Barbera started out making Tom and Jerry at MGM.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Daffy Duck: Daffy belongs to Warner Bros. and debuted in 1937, while Hanna-Barbera's own first stars, Tom and Jerry, came from MGM.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Mickey Mouse: Mickey is Disney's, not Hanna-Barbera's; he debuted in Steamboat Willie in 1928, decades before The Flintstones aired.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Popeye: Popeye was created by E. C. Segar in 1929, and his famous cartoons came from Fleischer Studios, not Hanna-Barbera.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Woody Woodpecker: Woody Woodpecker is Walter Lantz's creation from 1940, in cartoons released by Universal, not Hanna-Barbera.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Garfield: Garfield is Jim Davis's lasagna-loving cat from 1978, and his animated shows came from other studios, not Hanna-Barbera.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Snoopy: Snoopy is Charles Schulz's beagle, and Peanuts TV specials were produced by Bill Melendez.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Mighty Mouse: Mighty Mouse comes from Terrytoons, debuting in 1942 as 'Super Mouse', and has no link to Hanna-Barbera.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Underdog: Underdog is a 1960s hero, created for General Mills cereal commercials, and not by Hanna-Barbera.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Rocky: Rocky the flying squirrel is from the Jay Ward studio, which made his show with Bullwinkle.
Hanna-Barbera characters.Bullwinkle: Bullwinkle the moose is from the Jay Ward studio's Rocky and Bullwinkle, a 1959 show, rather than Hanna-Barbera.

Films set in London.Mary Poppins: The nanny arrives on Cherry Tree Lane, a made-up Edwardian London street; author P. L. Travers famously disliked Disney's version.
Films set in London.Paddington: The bear is named for London's Paddington station, where a bronze statue of him now waits on the concourse.
Films set in London.Notting Hill: The film's famous blue door belonged to a real house, and after a charity auction its owners repainted it black.
Films set in London.Love Actually: Interwoven Christmas stories mostly set in London, bookended by genuine arrival-gate hugs filmed with real travelers at Heathrow.
Films set in London.101 Dalmatians: Disney's 1961 cartoon helped pioneer xerography, copying drawings onto cels so animators never hand-inked every spot.
Films set in London.Oliver!: The 1968 musical based on Dickens's Oliver Twist won Best Picture, and shows the grimy streets of Victorian London.
Films set in London.The King's Speech: Colin Firth's King George VI conquers a stammer with therapist Lionel Logue; the film won four Oscars including Best Picture.
Films set in London.My Fair Lady: Eliza Doolittle's Covent Garden flower stall is the start; Audrey Hepburn's singing was largely dubbed by Marni Nixon.
Films set in London.Kingsman: The spy agency hides behind a tailor shop on Savile Row, London's famous street for bespoke suits.
Films set in London.About Time: Rachel McAdams's character meets Tim at a London restaurant where diners eat in total darkness, served by blind waiters.
Films set in London.Sherlock Holmes: Holmes lives at 221B Baker Street, an address that did not exist in Conan Doyle's day; a museum there now claims it.
Films set in London.Hot Fuzz: It opens in London, but a hotshot cop is transferred to sleepy Sandford, so nearly all of it takes place in the fictional village.
Films set in London.In Bruges: Two hitmen hide out in a Belgian canal city; London appears only in their bleak backstory.
Films set in London.Braveheart: Mel Gibson's William Wallace story is set in medieval Scotland, though much of it was filmed in Ireland.
Films set in London.Ratatouille: This one is Paris, where the rat Remy dreams of cooking; its stuffy critic Anton Ego is won over by a humble peasant dish.
Films set in London.Roman Holiday: A runaway princess explores Rome on a Vespa; the scooter scenes helped make the Vespa an icon of Italy.
Films set in London.Amelie: A quirky tale of Montmartre, so Paris; London is nowhere in it.
Films set in London.Casablanca: The line 'Play it again, Sam' is never actually spoken in this Morocco-set classic.
Films set in London.Midnight in Paris: Set in Paris, though Woody Allen has also made London films such as Match Point and Scoop.
Films set in London.Mamma Mia!: A Greek island musical whose stage show premiered in London's West End in 1999, the only London link.
Films set in London.Billy Elliot: Set in County Durham during the 1984 miners' strike; the boy's ballet audition is the only trip to London.
Films set in London.Local Hero: A Texas oil man visits a Scottish village, and the film's score came from Mark Knopfler of Dire Straits.
Films set in London.Brave: Pixar's Scotland: it was the studio's first fairy tale and its first film with a female lead.
Films set in London.Lost in Translation: Bill Murray's weary actor is stranded in Tokyo; the film won Sofia Coppola an Oscar for original screenplay.

Hogwarts teachers.Dumbledore: He taught Transfiguration before becoming headmaster, and Albus is Latin for white.
Hogwarts teachers.Snape: He teaches Potions, then Defense; Alan Rickman reportedly learned Snape's secret before readers because Rowling told him.
Hogwarts teachers.McGonagall: She teaches Transfiguration and can turn into a tabby cat with markings around her eyes like her glasses.
Hogwarts teachers.Lupin: Remus Lupin taught Defense Against the Dark Arts, and his name nods to the Latin for wolf.
Hogwarts teachers.Flitwick: The Charms teacher is a former dueling champion, and he is quite short in stature.
Hogwarts teachers.Sprout: Head of Hufflepuff and Herbology teacher, she grows the screaming mandrakes that cure petrification.
Hogwarts teachers.Trelawney: The Divination teacher made the real prophecy about Voldemort's downfall, though she never remembers doing so.
Hogwarts teachers.Lockhart: A fraud who takes credit for others' deeds, he lost his memory when his own backfired Memory Charm hit him.
Hogwarts teachers.Slughorn: The Potions master collects well-connected students into the Slug Club, and he returns in the sixth book.
Hogwarts teachers.Quirrell: His turban hides Voldemort's face on the back of his head, and he is the Defense teacher in book one.
Hogwarts teachers.Umbridge: Her pink cardigans and kitten plates hide a cruel High Inquisitor of Hogwarts who bans student groups.
Hogwarts teachers.Binns: The History of Magic teacher is a ghost who never noticed he died; he simply got up and left his body behind.
Hogwarts teachers.Hagrid: Hagrid teaches Care of Magical Creatures from the third book on, as well as keeping the grounds and keys.
Hogwarts teachers.Filch: Trap: the caretaker is a Squib, someone born to magical parents who can't do magic; he is no teacher.
Hogwarts teachers.Madam Pomfrey: The school nurse mends bones in seconds, though regrowing Harry's arm bones with Skele-Gro costs him a miserable night.
Hogwarts teachers.Madam Pince: The librarian guards the Restricted Section jealously, but she is not a teacher.
Hogwarts teachers.Cornelius Fudge: The Minister for Magic wears a bowler hat and refuses to believe Voldemort has returned.
Hogwarts teachers.Kingsley Shacklebolt: An Auror who becomes Minister for Magic after the war; he never taught at Hogwarts.
Hogwarts teachers.Sirius Black: Harry's godfather was a Hogwarts student and escaped from Azkaban, but he never taught there.
Hogwarts teachers.Arthur Weasley: Ron's father works at the Ministry and adores Muggle plugs; he isn't a teacher.
Hogwarts teachers.Lucius Malfoy: Draco's father is a school governor who got Dumbledore temporarily suspended in the second book.
Hogwarts teachers.Ollivander: The wand maker's Diagon Alley shop sign claims 'makers of fine wands since 382 B.C.'
Hogwarts teachers.Rita Skeeter: A gossip journalist at the Daily Prophet; she is secretly an unregistered Animagus who turns into a beetle.
Hogwarts teachers.Dobby: A house-elf freed with a sock; he dies in Deathly Hallows saving Harry and his friends.

Butlers from film and TV.Alfred: Alfred Pennyworth has served the Waynes since Bruce's childhood, and in some versions he is a former soldier or actor.
Butlers from film and TV.Jeeves: P. G. Wodehouse's unflappable valet is so famous that the search engine Ask Jeeves was named after him in 1996.
Butlers from film and TV.Carson: Downton Abbey's head butler, played by Jim Carter, guards tradition so firmly that new gadgets such as the telephone make him wary.
Butlers from film and TV.Geoffrey: Joseph Marcell played the dry English butler to the Banks family in The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, trading barbs with Will.
Butlers from film and TV.Lurch: The Addams Family's towering butler groans 'You rang?' and was played by Ted Cassidy, who stood about 6 ft 9 in.
Butlers from film and TV.Niles: The sharp-tongued butler in The Nanny, played by Daniel Davis, trades insults with the scheming C.C. Babcock.
Butlers from film and TV.Benson: Robert Guillaume won an Emmy for playing him in Soap, and the sassy butler was so popular that he got his own spin-off.
Butlers from film and TV.Cadbury: The Richie Rich butler, played by Jonathan Hyde in the 1994 film, keeps the world's richest boy out of trouble.
Butlers from film and TV.Hobson: Sir John Gielgud won a Best Supporting Actor Oscar for playing the acid-tongued valet in 1981's Arthur.
Butlers from film and TV.Fran Fine: A nanny, not a butler: Fran Drescher's brash Queens girl who lands with the Sheffield family in The Nanny.
Butlers from film and TV.Mary Poppins: A flying nanny, not a butler. P. L. Travers, her creator, was famously unhappy with Disney's film version.
Butlers from film and TV.Alice: The Brady family housekeeper, played by Ann B. Davis, was a live-in maid and cook rather than a butler.
Butlers from film and TV.Rosie: The Jetsons' robot maid does the housework, but she's a maid, not a butler. She's known for her sassy lines.
Butlers from film and TV.Mrs. Doubtfire: Robin Williams plays a dad who disguises himself as an old Scottish housekeeper, which is closer to a nanny than a butler.
Butlers from film and TV.Nanny McPhee: Emma Thompson wrote and played the magical nanny, whose warts and teeth fade as the children behave better.
Butlers from film and TV.Florence: Florence Johnston, played by Marla Gibbs on The Jeffersons, was a wisecracking maid rather than a butler.
Butlers from film and TV.Mrs. Hughes: The Downton Abbey housekeeper runs the female staff, a separate role from the butler, but she's Carson's closest ally.
Butlers from film and TV.Igor: A hunchbacked lab assistant in Frankenstein tales, and the 'Ygor' in the 1939 film was a role, not a butler's.
Butlers from film and TV.Smithers: Mr. Burns's devoted assistant in The Simpsons works as an executive assistant, not a butler, but he's equally loyal.
Butlers from film and TV.Renfield: Dracula's insect-eating servant is a lunatic, and he is a thrall rather than a proper butler.
Butlers from film and TV.Mr. Smee: Captain Hook's bumbling boatswain in Peter Pan is a pirate, not a butler, though he does serve his boss loyally.
Butlers from film and TV.Dobby: A Harry Potter house-elf who is bound to serve a family until it presents him with clothes, and he is a servant, not a butler.
Butlers from film and TV.Mrs. Potts: The teapot in Beauty and the Beast is a kindly housekeeper, voiced by Angela Lansbury, who also sang the title song.
Butlers from film and TV.Jiminy Cricket: Pinocchio's conscience is a cricket, not a butler, though Disney made him the film's guide and narrator.

Stage musicals based on films.Hairspray: The 1988 John Waters film became a 2002 Broadway hit that won eight Tonys. It was filmed again as a musical in 2007.
Stage musicals based on films.The Lion King: Disney's 1994 animated film became a 1997 stage show known for Julie Taymor's puppets. It is among the highest-grossing Broadway productions ever.
Stage musicals based on films.Legally Blonde: The 2001 comedy with Reese Witherspoon became a 2007 musical. A reality TV show was even used to cast its lead for the West End.
Stage musicals based on films.Mean Girls: Tina Fey adapted her own 2004 screenplay for Broadway in 2018. She wrote the book, and her husband Jeff Richmond wrote the music.
Stage musicals based on films.Beetlejuice: Tim Burton's 1988 comic-horror film became a 2019 Broadway musical. It leans into the film's gothic humor and sandworm sets.
Stage musicals based on films.School of Rock: Andrew Lloyd Webber wrote this 2015 stage version of the 2003 Jack Black film. Child actors play their own instruments live on stage.
Stage musicals based on films.Billy Elliot: The 2000 film about a miner's son who wants to dance became an Elton John musical. It won ten Tony Awards in 2009.
Stage musicals based on films.The Producers: Mel Brooks turned his 1967 film into a 2001 Broadway smash. It won a record twelve Tony Awards, which still stands.
Stage musicals based on films.Mrs. Doubtfire: The 1993 Robin Williams comedy reached Broadway in 2021, after its first run was cut short by the pandemic. A quick-change costume trick is central.
Stage musicals based on films.Footloose: The 1984 film about a town banning dancing was based on a real Oklahoma town. It was adapted into a musical in 1998.
Stage musicals based on films.Groundhog Day: The 1993 Bill Murray film was adapted by Tim Minchin in 2016. The musical keeps the time-loop premise and has a surprisingly sweet finish.
Stage musicals based on films.Les Misérables: This musical is adapted from Victor Hugo's novel, not a film. It premiered in Paris in 1980, then London in 1985.
Stage musicals based on films.Wicked: Based on Gregory Maguire's 1995 novel, which retells The Wizard of Oz. It is a book adaptation, not a film one.
Stage musicals based on films.Hamilton: Lin-Manuel Miranda drew on Ron Chernow's biography of Alexander Hamilton. It came from a book, not a movie.
Stage musicals based on films.Cats: Lloyd Webber set T. S. Eliot's poems to music in 1981. The film came decades later, after the stage show, so the order is reversed.
Stage musicals based on films.Oliver!: Lionel Bart's 1960 musical comes from Dickens's novel Oliver Twist. The film was made later, in 1968, and won Best Picture.
Stage musicals based on films.Matilda: The musical is based on Roald Dahl's 1988 book. Tim Minchin wrote the songs, and a film followed later, so it is not film-based.
Stage musicals based on films.Chicago: It started as a 1926 play by a crime reporter, then became a 1975 stage musical. The famous film came in 2002, after the show.
Stage musicals based on films.Rent: Jonathan Larson loosely based it on Puccini's opera La Bohème. He died the night before its first Off-Broadway preview.
Stage musicals based on films.Grease: It premiered on stage in Chicago in 1971, well before the 1978 John Travolta film. The film came from the musical, not the other way round.
Stage musicals based on films.West Side Story: It reworks Romeo and Juliet in 1950s New York and began on stage in 1957. The famous film arrived afterward in 1961.
Stage musicals based on films.Annie: The musical comes from the Little Orphan Annie comic strip, which began in 1924. The show opened in 1977, well before the 1982 film.
Stage musicals based on films.The Sound of Music: The 1959 stage show came first, based on Maria von Trapp's memoir. The beloved 1965 film adapted the musical, not vice versa.
Stage musicals based on films.Evita: Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice released it as a concept album in 1976 before staging it. The Madonna film came much later, in 1996.

Words to do with sound.Decibel: Named for Alexander Graham Bell, this unit is logarithmic, and a 10-decibel rise sounds about twice as loud.
Words to do with sound.Echo: Named after a nymph of Greek myth, and for a distinct echo, you generally need a surface about 17 meters away.
Words to do with sound.Acoustics: From Greek akouein, 'to hear'; it covers how rooms treat sound, so concert halls are designed around it.
Words to do with sound.Sonar: An acronym for sound navigation and ranging, used by ships and submarines.
Words to do with sound.Ultrasound: Sound above 20,000 hertz; doctors use it to look at unborn babies, and bats use it to hunt.
Words to do with sound.Sonic boom: The crack made when an object passes the speed of sound; Chuck Yeager first did so in 1947.
Words to do with sound.Reverb: Studios used to fake it with metal plates, springs and even echo chambers like bathrooms.
Words to do with sound.Infrasound: Below 20 hertz, too low for people, but elephants and whales use it to communicate.
Words to do with sound.Sound wave: Sound travels about 343 meters per second in air, and about four times faster in water.
Words to do with sound.Earshot: A distance measured by hearing: if someone's out of it, they can't hear you.
Words to do with sound.Audible: Human hearing spans roughly 20 to 20,000 hertz, and the top end shrinks with age.
Words to do with sound.Lumen: Lumens measure how much light a bulb gives off; sound is measured in decibels, a different scale from brightness.
Words to do with sound.Watt: The watt, named for James Watt, rates power; a loudspeaker has watts, but a watt isn't a measure of sound.
Words to do with sound.Volt: The volt, named for Alessandro Volta, measures electrical push; he invented the first battery in 1800.
Words to do with sound.Pixel: Pixel is short for picture element, the dots making up a screen image; it belongs to sight, not hearing.
Words to do with sound.Calorie: A calorie is a unit of heat energy; the food Calorie on labels is really 1,000 of them, and neither is about sound.
Words to do with sound.Lux: Lux measures light falling on a surface; a bright sunny day delivers around 100,000 of them, nothing to do with sound.
Words to do with sound.Kelvin: Kelvin starts at absolute zero, about minus 273 degrees Celsius; it measures temperature, not sound.
Words to do with sound.Photon: A photon is a packet of light; light is silent, and its speed vastly outruns sound.
Words to do with sound.Newton: The newton measures force; it's named for Isaac Newton, whose work on waves is no help here.
Words to do with sound.Joule: A joule, named for James Prescott Joule, measures energy; about one joule lifts an apple one meter.
Words to do with sound.Ohm: The ohm measures electrical resistance, named for Georg Ohm; it sounds musical, but it isn't about sound.
Words to do with sound.Megabyte: A megabyte is a million bytes of data; a minute of MP3 music takes up about one of them, but it isn't sound itself.
Words to do with sound.Horsepower: James Watt coined horsepower to sell steam engines by comparing them with draft horses; it measures power, not sound.

Rugby terms.Scrum: A scrum packs eight forwards from each side together to restart play, and the pushing contest can generate more than a tonne of force.
Rugby terms.Try: A try is worth five points and gets its name because it originally earned only a chance, a try, at a kick at goal.
Rugby terms.Lineout: A lineout restarts play after the ball goes into touch, and teammates lift a jumper to catch the throw-in.
Rugby terms.Conversion: A conversion is a kick worth two points taken after a try, taken from in line with where the ball was grounded.
Rugby terms.Ruck: A ruck forms over a tackled player on the ground, and players cannot use their hands to take the ball.
Rugby terms.Maul: A maul forms when a player carrying the ball is held up by opponents and teammates bind around him, and it can roll forward.
Rugby terms.Knock-on: A knock-on is when the ball goes forward off a player's hand or arm, resulting in a scrum to the opposition.
Rugby terms.Drop goal: A drop goal is worth three points and is kicked in open play after the ball bounces; Jonny Wilkinson scored one to win the 2003 World Cup.
Rugby terms.Fly-half: The fly-half wears 10 and is the playmaker who directs the attack, and the role is called the first five-eighth in New Zealand.
Rugby terms.Prop: The prop is a front-row forward who supports the hooker in the scrum, and they're often the strongest players on the team.
Rugby terms.Garryowen: A Garryowen is a high kick that lets chasers race for the ball, named after a Limerick rugby club.
Rugby terms.Touchdown: A touchdown is American football's, but in rugby the ball must be pressed down to ground it for a try, hence the name.
Rugby terms.Home run: A home run is baseball's, and rugby tries are worth five, not four, points.
Rugby terms.Puck: A puck is hockey's, and the rugby ball is oval with four panels and is meant to be kicked and carried.
Rugby terms.Icing: Icing is hockey's rule, and rugby has no such rule against kicking long.
Rugby terms.Slam dunk: A slam dunk is basketball's, and a rugby player may pass only backward or sideways.
Rugby terms.Wicket: A wicket is cricket's; rugby's goalposts are an H shape, and conversions go between the uprights and over the bar.
Rugby terms.Birdie: A birdie is golf's one under par, not a rugby feature.
Rugby terms.Deuce: Deuce is tennis's 40-all, and rugby's tie-break in knockouts is extra time, then sudden death kicks.
Rugby terms.Bunt: A bunt is baseball's tap; rugby's nearest is the grubber kick, a low ball kicked along the ground.
Rugby terms.Free throw: A free throw is basketball's; rugby's free kick is a different restart and awarded for minor infringements.
Rugby terms.Corner kick: A corner kick is soccer's; rugby has no such restart because the ball is pushed back, not played to corners.
Rugby terms.Checkmate: Checkmate is chess's end; rugby borrows the strategic talk, with sides planning phases of play like moves in a game.
Rugby terms.Gutter ball: A gutter ball is bowling's, and rugby's nearest equivalent is a poor kick that goes dead.

Scuba diving gear.Mask: It needs a nose pocket so divers can pinch the nose and equalize pressure as they descend.
Scuba diving gear.Snorkel: A curved breathing tube for the surface, which divers don't use underwater, since it can't supply air at depth.
Scuba diving gear.Fins: Their blade shape lets a diver move far more efficiently than with legs alone.
Scuba diving gear.Wetsuit: Made of neoprene, it traps a thin layer of water that the body warms.
Scuba diving gear.Regulator: Cousteau and Gagnan's 1943 Aqua-Lung used one to cut tank pressure to a level a diver can breathe.
Scuba diving gear.Air tank: It holds ordinary compressed air, about 21 percent oxygen, rather than pure oxygen.
Scuba diving gear.BCD: This inflatable vest lets divers hover neutrally and also helps them float at the surface.
Scuba diving gear.Dive computer: It tracks nitrogen absorption and so it warns divers when they risk decompression sickness.
Scuba diving gear.Weight belt: Lead weights offset the buoyancy of the wetsuit, so that a diver can sink.
Scuba diving gear.Depth gauge: A small gauge shows how deep a diver is, which matters because pressure rises with every 10 meters.
Scuba diving gear.Dive knife: Divers mostly use it as a tool for cutting tangled line, not as a weapon against sharks.
Scuba diving gear.Crampons: Crampons strap to boots for ice and snow, not underwater.
Scuba diving gear.Ice axe: An ice axe is for mountaineers, not for divers.
Scuba diving gear.Carabiner: Climbers use carabiners, and divers prefer stainless steel bolt snaps because aluminum corrodes in saltwater.
Scuba diving gear.Ski poles: Ski poles balance skiers, but divers move with fins and not with poles.
Scuba diving gear.Parachute: A parachute is for skydivers, a name that sounds similar but a different sport.
Scuba diving gear.Oar: An oar is rowing gear, and does not work underwater.
Scuba diving gear.Paddle: A paddle is for kayaks and canoes, which stay on the surface.
Scuba diving gear.Surfboard: A surfboard keeps a rider on the surface, while scuba is about going below.
Scuba diving gear.Bobber: A bobber floats on a fishing line and doesn't help with diving.
Scuba diving gear.Racket: A racket is for tennis or squash, and not for diving.
Scuba diving gear.Saddle: A saddle is for horses or bikes, and is useless on a dive.
Scuba diving gear.Shin guards: Shin guards protect soccer players from kicks, not divers.
Scuba diving gear.Chalk bag: A chalk bag is for rock climbers and would dissolve in water.

Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Love: In tennis, love means zero, and a popular but unproven theory links it to the French l'oeuf, meaning egg.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Nil: In football and many other sports, nil is how you say a team scored nothing.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Duck: In cricket, a duck means a batter out without scoring, short for duck's egg, from the shape of a zero.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Goose egg: A goose egg is American slang for a zero on the scoreboard, like a baseball inning with no runs.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Bagel: In tennis, winning a set 6-0 is called a bagel, the shape of the zero.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Zip: Zip is slang for zero and also the sound of nothing, as in 'beat 3-zip'.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Zilch: Zilch is slang for nothing, possibly from the name of a comic character, according to some sources.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Nada: Nada is Spanish for 'nothing' and is widely used in English as a casual zero.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Zero: Zero is from Arabic sifr via Italian, which also gave us 'cipher'.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Ace: An ace in tennis is a serve the opponent never touches, and in cards it counts as one or eleven, so it is a point scored, never zero.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Deuce: Deuce means 40-all in tennis, from the French deux, since a player must win two points in a row to take the game.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Birdie: A birdie is one stroke under par in golf. The term came from early 1900s American slang, where 'bird' meant something excellent.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Eagle: An eagle is two strokes under par in golf, and it's rarer than a birdie; three under par is the even rarer albatross.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Par: Par is the number of strokes an expert is expected to need on a hole, so scoring par is far from nothing: it is the baseline.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Hat trick: Three goals by one player in a game is a hat trick, a term from cricket, where a bowler earned a hat for three wickets in a row.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Century: A century is 100 runs in cricket, the opposite of zero, and scoring one in a Test is a career milestone for any batter.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Strike: A strike in bowling knocks down all ten pins with the first ball. It's the best result of a frame, not the worst.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Spare: A spare in bowling means clearing the remaining pins with a second ball in a frame, which earns a bonus of the next roll.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Turkey: A turkey is three consecutive strikes in bowling, a name some say began when alley owners gave away turkeys as prizes.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Tie: A tie means equal scores, which can include 0-0, but the word itself says nothing about the number of points.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Double: A double means two of something, such as a baseball two-base hit or doubling a score in darts, but never zero.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Single: A single is one point or one base hit, as in baseball, the lowest scoring hit besides none at all.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Triple: A triple is a three-base hit in baseball, a rare feat because it requires speed and a deep drive.
Ways to say zero (in sport and beyond).Treble: Treble is the narrow ring on a dartboard that triples the score, so a treble 20 gets 60 points, the maximum for three darts' worth.

Found in a standard 52-card deck.Ace: The ace plays high or low, and in cards it's rank one. Its name comes from the Latin 'as', a unit of coin, and it often beats a king.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.King: Kings carry a sword or a symbol of power, and the King of Hearts, famously, is shown without a moustache and stabbing himself with a sword.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Queen: The queen was added to Western decks in the 15th century, and she is the only face card without a standard weapon.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Jack: The Jack was once the 'knave', a servant, and its name changed because the letter K clashed with 'king' in abbreviations.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Hearts: Hearts are red and, in the game of Hearts, you want to avoid them, since each heart costs points.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Spades: The spade suit's name comes from the Italian spade, meaning swords, and spades are often the top suit in games like bridge.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Clubs: Clubs have a clover symbol, but the name comes from the Spanish and Italian suits' batons, not the clover.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Diamonds: Diamonds are the red suit that in Italian decks were coins, and in bridge they rank below hearts.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Ten: In a standard deck, a ten is worth ten in blackjack, like face cards, and it is the highest pip card.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Nine: Nines are the lowest card in some trick games like Pinochle and Euchre, where cards below nine are removed.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Deuce: The deuce is a two, from the French deux, and it's often the lowest card in a standard deck.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Knight: The knight is a face card in tarot and some European decks, and it's not in a standard 52-card deck.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Prince: Princes appear in some Asian and fantasy decks but not in a standard 52-card deck.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Bishop: Bishops are chess pieces, and no standard card has this rank.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Rook: Rooks are chess pieces, not playing cards.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Emperor: Emperor is a tarot trump card, not a card in a standard 52-card deck.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Swords: Swords are a suit in tarot and Latin decks, from which the spade was derived.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Cups: Cups are a tarot suit, from which the hearts derive.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Wands: Wands are a tarot suit, ancestors of the club suit.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Coins: Coins are a tarot suit that became diamonds.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Pentacles: Pentacles are the tarot version of coins, not part of the standard deck.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Stars: Stars are a suit in some alternative decks, though tarot has a Star card.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Crowns: Crowns are not a suit in a standard deck, and some decks use them.
Found in a standard 52-card deck.Princess: Princess is a court card in some tarot decks, but not in a standard 52-card deck.

Baseball legends.Babe Ruth: He started as a Red Sox pitcher, then became baseball's first superstar slugger, hitting 60 home runs in 1927 and drawing crowds everywhere.
Baseball legends.Hank Aaron: He broke Ruth's career home run record in 1974, finishing with 755, a mark that stood until 2007, while enduring racist threats.
Baseball legends.Willie Mays: The Say Hey Kid's over-the-shoulder catch in the 1954 World Series is called simply The Catch, and he hit 660 home runs.
Baseball legends.Derek Jeter: The Yankees captain spent his entire 20-year career in pinstripes and reached 3,000 hits with a home run.
Baseball legends.Jackie Robinson: He broke baseball's colour barrier in 1947, and his number 42 is retired across every Major League team, the only number so honoured.
Baseball legends.Lou Gehrig: The Iron Horse played 2,130 straight games until illness struck, and the disease, ALS, is still called Lou Gehrig's disease in the US.
Baseball legends.Ted Williams: He was the last major leaguer to hit .400 in a season, in 1941, and he also served as a fighter pilot in two wars.
Baseball legends.Mickey Mantle: The Yankees switch-hitter won the Triple Crown in 1956 and hit towering home runs from both sides of the plate.
Baseball legends.Shohei Ohtani: The Japanese star both pitches and hits at an elite level, and in 2024 he became the first player with 50 homers and 50 stolen bases.
