Baseball legends.Roberto Clemente: He collected 3,000 hits and was also a humanitarian, dying in a 1972 plane crash while delivering aid to Nicaragua.
Baseball legends.Joe DiMaggio: His 56-game hitting streak in 1941 is still the record, and it has never been seriously threatened since.
Baseball legends.Tom Brady: A quarterback with seven Super Bowl titles, he was also drafted by the Montreal Expos in 1995, but chose football.
Baseball legends.Wayne Gretzky: Hockey's all-time leading scorer, he did not play baseball, though he threw out a first pitch or two.
Baseball legends.Kobe Bryant: He spent his whole career with the Lakers and scored 81 points in a single game, in basketball.
Baseball legends.Jerry Rice: The all-time NFL receiving leader caught passes, not fastballs, and starred for the 49ers.
Baseball legends.Pele: The only man to win three World Cups, he scored over a thousand goals and is a football icon, not a baseball one.
Baseball legends.Tiger Woods: He's won 15 major golf championships, and his 1997 Masters victory came by a record margin of 12 strokes.
Baseball legends.Larry Bird: A Celtics forward known for deadly shooting, who won three straight NBA MVP awards in the 1980s.
Baseball legends.Joe Montana: A San Francisco 49ers quarterback with four Super Bowl wins, and he threw footballs, not curveballs.
Baseball legends.Walter Payton: A Chicago Bears running back who rushed for over 16,000 yards, and who was known for his punishing running style.
Baseball legends.Magic Johnson: The Lakers point guard, 6 foot 9, revolutionized the position and announced he was HIV positive in 1991, a moment that changed public attitudes.
Baseball legends.Bill Russell: The Celtics centre won 11 NBA championships in 13 seasons, the most any player has ever won, and he was the first Black head coach in the league.

Egyptian gods.Ra: The sun god who sailed across the sky by day and through the underworld by night. Pharaohs claimed to be his sons.
Egyptian gods.Osiris: God of the dead and rebirth, killed by his brother Set. His green skin shows renewal, linked to the Nile's regrowth.
Egyptian gods.Isis: The great goddess of magic and motherhood, who reassembled Osiris. Her worship spread across the Roman world.
Egyptian gods.Horus: The falcon-headed sky god, son of Isis and Osiris. Pharaohs were seen as living Horuses, and his eye symbolized protection.
Egyptian gods.Anubis: The jackal-headed god of embalming who weighed hearts of the dead. The black color stood for the rich soil of the Nile, not death.
Egyptian gods.Set: God of chaos, storms and the desert. He murdered Osiris in myth, but he also defended Ra's boat against the serpent Apep.
Egyptian gods.Thoth: Ibis-headed god of writing, wisdom and the moon. He recorded the result when a heart was weighed against a feather.
Egyptian gods.Bastet: The cat-headed goddess of home and protection. Cats were so sacred that harming one could be punished harshly.
Egyptian gods.Ptah: Creator god of Memphis and patron of craftsmen. Egypt's name may come from a Greek version of his temple's name.
Egyptian gods.Hathor: Goddess of love, music and joy, shown with cow horns. Her temple at Dendera is among Egypt's best preserved.
Egyptian gods.Sobek: The crocodile-headed god of the Nile, linked with strength and fertility. A temple at Kom Ombo honors him.
Egyptian gods.Zeus: The Greek king of the gods. Egypt has no match, though Greeks equated him with the Egyptian god Amun.
Egyptian gods.Odin: The one-eyed Norse chief god, who rules from Asgard. He comes from Scandinavia, not from the banks of the Nile.
Egyptian gods.Thor: A Norse thunder god who wields a hammer. He has no place in Egypt's pantheon, which is far from Scandinavia.
Egyptian gods.Hera: The Greek queen of the gods and wife of Zeus. She belongs to Mount Olympus rather than to Egypt's pantheon.
Egyptian gods.Marduk: The patron god of Babylon in Mesopotamia. He is near Egypt geographically but belongs to a different religion.
Egyptian gods.Quetzalcoatl: The Aztec feathered serpent god of wind and learning. He's from Mesoamerica, an ocean away.
Egyptian gods.Cleopatra: The last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, who died in 30 BC. She was a queen, though she was worshipped as a living Isis.
Egyptian gods.Tutankhamun: A boy pharaoh whose tomb was found nearly intact in 1922. He was a king, not a god, although kings became divine in death.
Egyptian gods.Ramses II: One of Egypt's greatest pharaohs, who ruled for 66 years. He was a king and not a god, but he built vast temples to the gods.
Egyptian gods.Nefertiti: The queen of Akhenaten, famed for her painted bust now in Berlin. She was royal and powerful, but not a deity.
Egyptian gods.Mars: The Roman god of war, and the namesake of the red planet. He belongs to Rome, not to Egypt's pantheon.
Egyptian gods.Apollo: The Greek god of the sun and music. He isn't Egyptian, though Greeks linked Horus with him.
Egyptian gods.Hammurabi: A Babylonian king famed for his law code, about 1750 BC. He was a human ruler of Mesopotamia, not an Egyptian god.

Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Cats: Revered for the goddess Bastet. Millions of cat mummies were found, and killing a cat was punished harshly.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Ibises: Sacred to the god Thoth, they were mummified in huge numbers at Saqqara, with over a million found there.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Crocodiles: Sacred to Sobek. Mummified crocodiles have been found at Kom Ombo, some adults, others hatchlings.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Baboons: Sacred to Thoth as well, baboons were mummified. Researchers used their mummies to trace the location of the lost land of Punt.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Dogs: Often mummified in huge numbers, as the god Anubis was jackal-headed, and dogs were buried by their owners too.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Falcons: Revered as images of Horus, millions of falcons were mummified, and they were found by the thousand at ancient animal cemeteries.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Bulls: The Apis bull was seen as a living god in Memphis. When one died, it was mummified and entombed in a huge stone sarcophagus.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Shrews: Shrews were mummified, as they were sacred to Horus in some forms. Tiny bronze coffins, some with shrew mummies, survive.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Snakes: Snakes, including cobras, were mummified and buried as offerings, and linked to goddess Wadjet, whose symbol appears on pharaohs' crowns.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Fish: Nile perch were mummified at Esna and linked to the goddess Neith, and they were wrapped as offerings.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Gazelles: Gazelles were mummified, sometimes as food offerings so the dead would have meat in the afterlife.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Scarab beetles: Sacred scarabs symbolized the rising sun, with the dung beetle pushing a ball like the sun across the sky.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Kangaroos: Trap: Australian marsupials, and Egyptians never saw one. Wrong continent entirely.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Penguins: Trap: penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere, and no ancient Egyptian ever met one.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Tigers: Trap: tigers are Asian big cats, and the Egyptians never kept them. They did, however, mummify lions.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Turkeys: Trap: turkeys are a New World bird, unknown to Egyptians. The mummified birds were ibises and falcons.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Bison: Trap: bison are American and European, and not found in Egypt. Egyptians mummified bulls instead.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Pandas: Trap: pandas live in bamboo forests in China, far from the Nile, so Egyptians never mummified one.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Llamas: Trap: llamas are from the Andes, thousands of miles from Egypt, so none were ever mummified there.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Polar bears: Trap: polar bears live in the Arctic, thousands of miles from Egypt, so none were mummified.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Koalas: Trap: koalas live only in Australia, so no ancient Egyptian ever saw one, let alone mummified it.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Armadillos: Trap: armadillos are from the Americas, which Egyptians never reached, so none were mummified.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Moose: Trap: moose live in northern forests, far from the Nile. Egypt's mummified animals were local.
Animals ancient Egyptians mummified.Platypuses: Trap: platypuses are Australian egg-laying mammals and were completely unknown to Egyptians.

Titles of nobility.Duke: The word comes from Latin dux, 'leader', which Roman generals once bore before it became the top noble rank below royalty.
Titles of nobility.Earl: Britain's oldest title, with no feminine form of its own; an earl's wife is a countess.
Titles of nobility.Baron: The lowest rank of the British peerage, yet it was barons who forced King John to sign Magna Carta in 1215.
Titles of nobility.Count: The word for a count's land gave us 'county'; in Britain the equivalent title is earl.
Titles of nobility.Marquess: Originally lord of a borderland, or march, where defense meant extra power.
Titles of nobility.Viscount: The name means 'vice-count', a count's deputy, and it's pronounced 'VYE-count', with a silent s.
Titles of nobility.Archduke: The title unique to Habsburgs; Franz Ferdinand's assassination in 1914 was the spark for World War I.
Titles of nobility.Duchess: The wife of a duke, though women like Anne of Brittany held duchies in their own right.
Titles of nobility.Countess: Ada Lovelace, often called the first computer programmer, was also a countess.
Titles of nobility.Serf: Bound to the land they worked, serfs couldn't leave a manor without the lord's permission.
Titles of nobility.Peasant: They were the majority of medieval Europeans, and they were farmers with no title.
Titles of nobility.Squire: A squire was a knight's attendant, so a rank below a knight and not a noble title proper.
Titles of nobility.Yeoman: A free farmer who owned land, though not noble; Yeomen of the Guard still guard the Tower of London.
Titles of nobility.Villein: A villein was an unfree tenant farmer, and the word 'villain' grew from it.
Titles of nobility.Page: A boy of about seven sent to a noble household to begin training for knighthood.
Titles of nobility.Merchant: Rich merchants could outearn nobles, but money didn't buy a title in the Middle Ages.
Titles of nobility.Jester: Court jesters were sometimes the only people allowed to mock the king, but they held no rank.
Titles of nobility.Monk: Monks belonged to the Church, though many came from noble families.
Titles of nobility.Friar: Unlike monks, friars begged and traveled; Friar Tuck is the famous fictional one.
Titles of nobility.Reeve: The manor official who supervised peasants' work; a 'shire-reeve' became the word sheriff.
Titles of nobility.Shepherd: A shepherd tended sheep whose wool was England's chief medieval export.
Titles of nobility.Blacksmith: A blacksmith was essential to village life, and Smith is still among England's most common surnames.
Titles of nobility.Bailiff: An estate manager under the lord; the sheriff's bailiwick comes from the same word.
Titles of nobility.Miller: Lords often owned the mill and forced peasants to use it and pay a share, which made millers unpopular.

Things in a sewing kit.Needle: Bone needles about 50,000 years old have been found in Denisova Cave in Siberia, making sewing far older than farming.
Things in a sewing kit.Thread: Silk thread comes from a single cocoon filament that can run for nearly a kilometer without a break.
Things in a sewing kit.Thimble: The word began as 'thumb bell', since the earliest thimbles were worn on the thumb before moving to the finger.
Things in a sewing kit.Pins: Pins were once so precious that husbands gave wives 'pin money', and modern ones get glass heads so they can be found.
Things in a sewing kit.Pincushion: Many are stuffed with wool, because the lanolin in it helps keep pins from rusting, and tomato shapes are traditional.
Things in a sewing kit.Safety pin: Walter Hunt patented it in 1849, said to have made it in a few hours to pay off a $15 debt.
Things in a sewing kit.Seam ripper: Sewers jokingly call using one 'reverse sewing'; its curved hook slides under a stitch while a tiny blade cuts the thread.
Things in a sewing kit.Buttons: The oldest known buttons, made of shell, come from Mohenjo-daro in the Indus Valley, about 5,000 years old.
Things in a sewing kit.Needle threader: A tiny diamond of wire pulled through the needle's eye, it spares you from squinting at an eye smaller than a grain of rice.
Things in a sewing kit.Fabric scissors: Sewers famously guard these: cutting paper dulls the blades fast, so family scissors are a classic domestic crime.
Things in a sewing kit.Tailor's chalk: Traditional chalk comes as a flat triangle of clay or talc, and the lines brush off the fabric afterward.
Things in a sewing kit.Stapler: A desk tool, though upholstery staple guns do tack fabric, so the staple does appear in upholstery workshops.
Things in a sewing kit.Nail: When Romans abandoned Inchtuthil in Scotland, they buried about 875,000 nails to keep them from the enemy; it's a hardware item, not sewing.
Things in a sewing kit.Screw: Archimedes is linked to the screw as a water-lifting device, though sewing relies on thread and needle.
Things in a sewing kit.Hammer: A hammer hits rather than stitches, a toolbox item that has no place among needles.
Things in a sewing kit.Paper clip: Sewers sometimes borrow clips on thick fabric, but a paper clip is not standard kit gear.
Things in a sewing kit.Rubber band: Elastic thread is in many kits, but a rubber band is stationery; elastic thread was once made from rubber too.
Things in a sewing kit.Thumbtack: A thumbtack is too thick to pass through fabric cleanly, so it stays in the stationery drawer.
Things in a sewing kit.Spatula: A kitchen utensil with no role in mending a hem; the name spatula comes from the Latin for a small flat blade.
Things in a sewing kit.Paintbrush: A brush applies paint, not stitches; some fabric paints do exist, but it won't turn up in a standard sewing box.
Things in a sewing kit.Highlighter: A highlighter marks printed text; tailors use chalk or fading pens to mark fabric instead.
Things in a sewing kit.Glue stick: A glue stick works on paper, but fabric needs thread, and most clothing glue is a specialized fabric adhesive.
Things in a sewing kit.Wrench: The British call it a spanner, and it tightens bolts rather than clothes.
Things in a sewing kit.Corkscrew: It spirals like a needle's twist but opens bottles, not seams.

Garden tools.Rake: Rakes were used by farmers for ages, and the leaf rake has flexible tines that gather debris without tearing the lawn.
Garden tools.Shovel: A shovel with a rounded point is for digging, while a flat-edged one is made for scooping, and the difference matters when moving soil.
Garden tools.Hoe: The hoe is one of the oldest farming tools, and it cuts weeds just below the soil, where roots meet stems.
Garden tools.Trowel: A garden trowel is a hand-sized scoop for planting bulbs and seedlings, and its handle was shaped for a steady grip.
Garden tools.Wheelbarrow: The wheelbarrow was used in China by around the first century, and it lets one person carry loads that would otherwise need two.
Garden tools.Garden hose: A hose with a leak can waste a lot of water, and a typical garden hose delivers roughly 9 gallons a minute.
Garden tools.Watering can: A watering can's rose, the perforated nozzle, spreads water in a gentle shower that won't blast seedlings out of the soil.
Garden tools.Pruning shears: Bypass pruners cut like scissors, while anvil ones crush against a flat plate, and bypass pruners give cleaner cuts on live wood.
Garden tools.Lawnmower: The first mower, invented in 1830, was inspired by a machine that trimmed cloth and was made for sports fields and gardens.
Garden tools.Leaf blower: The leaf blower was invented in Japan in the 1950s, intended originally for spraying pesticides.
Garden tools.Hedge trimmer: Hedge trimmers cut with a pair of reciprocating blades that slide over each other, like a long, fast scissors.
Garden tools.Garden fork: A garden fork has strong tines for loosening and turning compacted soil, and it is often used for lifting root crops like potatoes.
Garden tools.Weed whacker: A weed whacker, or string trimmer, was invented in the 1970s by a Texan, George Ballas, who got the idea from a car wash.
Garden tools.Spatula: A spatula belongs in the kitchen for flipping food, so it's a trap, and one with a flat blade can lift cookies.
Garden tools.Ladle: A ladle is a kitchen tool for serving soup, and the word comes from an Old English word for lifting.
Garden tools.Whisk: It's a kitchen tool, and a whisk's wire loops trap air in cream and eggs, so it has no garden job.
Garden tools.Mop: A mop cleans floors indoors, and some look like they could clear a garden path, but it is not a garden tool.
Garden tools.Plunger: A plunger clears blocked drains, and it works by pushing air and water in a plumbing line, not in a garden.
Garden tools.Stapler: A stapler binds paper, which you might use to staple garden labels, but it is an office tool.
Garden tools.Hair dryer: A hair dryer is for hair, though gardeners sometimes joke about it for thawing a frozen tap.
Garden tools.Ironing board: An ironing board is a household item for pressing clothes, and the gardener doesn't need it.
Garden tools.Toaster: A toaster browns bread, and the garden shed has no need of one.
Garden tools.Colander: A colander drains pasta, but it also appears in gardens as an improvised sieve for washing vegetables, though it's a kitchen tool.
Garden tools.Can opener: A can opener was invented decades after the can itself, in the 1850s, and it is a kitchen tool, not a garden one.

Things that have strings.Guitar: Standard guitar strings are tuned E A D G B E, and the thick low strings are wound with metal wire to add weight.
Things that have strings.Violin: A violin bow is strung with horsehair, which is rubbed with rosin so it grips the strings and makes them sing.
Things that have strings.Tennis racket: Most tennis strings today are synthetic, but traditional natural gut came from cow intestines, not cats.
Things that have strings.Marionette: A marionette is controlled from above by strings on a wooden bar, and the word is French for little Mary.
Things that have strings.Kite: Early Chinese kites flew over two thousand years ago and were used to measure distances and carry messages.
Things that have strings.Yo-yo: The yo-yo is said to have started as a Filipino hunting weapon, and a Filipino, Pedro Flores, started selling them in the US in the 1920s.
Things that have strings.Harp: A concert harp has 47 strings and seven pedals, and the pedals shift each string's pitch by a semitone.
Things that have strings.Archery bow: A bowstring is not elastic; the bow's limbs store the energy, and the string transfers it to the arrow.
Things that have strings.Banjo: The banjo grew out of instruments brought from West Africa, and its drum head gives its bright twang.
Things that have strings.Piano: Surprisingly, a piano counts as a string instrument, because its hammers strike strings; a grand has about 230 of them.
Things that have strings.Badminton racket: Badminton rackets are among the lightest in sport, often under 90 grams, and their strings are tightened hard to send the shuttle flying.
Things that have strings.Tea bag: A tea bag has a string so you can pull it out, and the tea bag itself came from a New York merchant who sent samples in silk bags.
Things that have strings.Cello: A cello is played seated with an endpin that rests on the floor, and its range sounds close to the human voice.
Things that have strings.Trumpet: A trumpet makes sound when the player's lips buzz into a mouthpiece, so it uses air, not strings.
Things that have strings.Flute: A flute works by blowing across a hole to split the air, and there is no string involved.
Things that have strings.Ping-pong paddle: A ping-pong paddle is a wood blade covered in rubber, with no strings, unlike a tennis racket.
Things that have strings.Baseball bat: A baseball bat is a solid piece of wood or aluminum with no strings, just a sweet spot.
Things that have strings.Golf club: A golf club has a shaft and a head, and the grooves on the face help spin the ball.
Things that have strings.Frisbee: A Frisbee is a molded plastic disc, which gets its lift from spinning through the air.
Things that have strings.Skateboard: A skateboard is a deck on four wheels, and it needs no string.
Things that have strings.Saxophone: A saxophone is a woodwind, not a string or a brass instrument, because it uses a single reed.
Things that have strings.Clarinet: A clarinet is also a reed instrument, and it is the only common woodwind that overblows at a twelfth.
Things that have strings.Xylophone: A xylophone has wooden bars, not strings; it is struck with mallets, and each bar makes one note.
Things that have strings.Hockey stick: A hockey stick is a shaft with a flat blade, with no strings, unlike a lacrosse stick.

Things used to erase a mistake.Eraser: Joseph Priestley noted in 1770 that rubber rubbed out pencil marks, and before that people used bread crumbs.
Things used to erase a mistake.Correction fluid: Secretary Bette Nesmith Graham invented it in the 1950s, and her son Michael Nesmith later became a member of The Monkees.
Things used to erase a mistake.Correction tape: The tape lays a dry white film over an error, so you can write over it immediately with no waiting for it to dry.
Things used to erase a mistake.Kneaded eraser: Artists mold this putty-like eraser into any shape, and it lifts graphite off the page instead of rubbing it away.
Things used to erase a mistake.Whiteboard eraser: Dry-erase ink sits on top of a nonporous surface, which is why a simple felt wipe lifts it right off.
Things used to erase a mistake.Chalkboard duster: Chalk is soft limestone or gypsum, and a duster just lifts the loose powder rather than dissolving anything.
Things used to erase a mistake.Eraser pen: A pen-shaped holder with a thin eraser rod makes tiny, precise corrections, even inside a single letter.
Things used to erase a mistake.White-out pen: A fine tip dabs correction fluid exactly where you need it, and you shake it first to mix the pigment.
Things used to erase a mistake.Eraser shield: This thin metal stencil has slots that expose only the spot you want to erase, protecting the rest of the drawing.
Things used to erase a mistake.Pen: Pilot's FriXion pens use heat-sensitive ink that vanishes with the friction of rubbing, but ordinary pens do not.
Things used to erase a mistake.Marker: Dry-erase markers can be wiped away, but permanent markers use inks that bond to a surface and resist erasing.
Things used to erase a mistake.Highlighter: Highlighter ink is translucent, so it adds color while the text underneath stays readable.
Things used to erase a mistake.Fountain pen: Water-based fountain pen ink soaks into paper fibers, which is why it is so hard to erase once it dries.
Things used to erase a mistake.Stapler: A stapler fastens papers together and needs a separate staple remover to undo its work.
Things used to erase a mistake.Crayon: Crayon is wax and pigment, built to resist smudging, so it is poor at erasing and good at making a mess.
Things used to erase a mistake.Glue stick: The glue stick was invented by Henkel in Germany in 1969, with the twist-up design inspired by lipstick.
Things used to erase a mistake.Ruler: The inch is said to come from the width of a thumb, and a ruler guides lines but removes nothing.
Things used to erase a mistake.Paper clip: During the Second World War, Norwegians wore paper clips on their lapels as a quiet sign of national unity.
Things used to erase a mistake.Hole punch: The little circles it cuts out are called chads, the same word made famous by the contested 2000 US election.
Things used to erase a mistake.Ink pad: An ink pad carries ink to a stamp, and it makes marks, not removes them.
Things used to erase a mistake.Rubber stamp: Vulcanized rubber made practical stamps possible, and a stamp leaves a permanent mark rather than erasing one.
Things used to erase a mistake.Sharpie: The Sharpie, introduced in 1964, was among the first permanent markers, and it is designed to defeat erasing.
Things used to erase a mistake.Hole reinforcer: These little sticky rings fix a torn hole on a ring-binder page, repairing the damage rather than erasing a mistake.
Things used to erase a mistake.Envelope: Before the 1840s, letters were usually folded and sealed, because postage in Britain was priced per sheet.

Things for cleaning your teeth.Toothbrush: Dentists suggest replacing it about every three months, and the first bristle brush is credited to China around 1498.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Toothpaste: Fluoride is the active ingredient that strengthens enamel, and the grit is mild abrasive, often silica, that lifts stains.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Dental floss: Levi Spear Parmly, a New Orleans dentist, recommended silk thread for teeth in 1815, and flossing reaches the tooth surfaces a brush misses.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Mouthwash: Mouthwash cannot replace brushing; it rinses and freshens, and some types add fluoride or antibacterial agents.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Tongue scraper: Tongue scraping goes back to ancient India, and it removes the coating that can cause bad breath.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Water flosser: The first water flosser was invented in the 1960s by a dentist and his patient, an engineer, in Colorado.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Interdental brush: These tiny bottle brushes come in sizes to match the gaps between teeth, and they suit wider spaces and braces.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Denture tablets: Fizzing tablets release oxygen bubbles that lift stains and bacteria, and dentures should still be brushed daily.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Whitening strips: Peroxide strips can lighten teeth by a few shades, though sensitivity is a common side effect.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Dental picks: Wooden or plastic picks go back to ancient times, and toothpicks were found among Neanderthal remains.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Lip balm: A trap: lip balm cares for lips and not teeth, and many were first made in the 1880s for chapped lips.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Nail file: A nail file shapes nails, and using it on teeth would damage the enamel, which is the hardest substance in the body.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Cotton swab: The cotton swab was invented in the 1920s by Leo Gerstenzang, and ear doctors warn against pushing one into the canal.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Earplugs: Foam earplugs were invented for hearing protection, and the ancient version used wax in Greek legend.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Eye drops: Eye drops are meant for the eyes, and they are sterile for that reason.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Nasal spray: Nasal sprays are for noses, and overusing decongestant ones can cause rebound congestion.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Cough drops: Cough drops soothe the throat, and many contain menthol, sugar and sometimes a bit of honey.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Lipstick: Ancient Mesopotamians crushed gemstones to color their lips, and it does nothing for teeth.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Deodorant: Deodorant masks smell and antiperspirant blocks sweat, so it belongs in the armpits.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Tweezers: Tweezers pluck hairs and splinters, and the word comes from an old French term for a small case.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Hand sanitizer: Sanitizer is usually 60 to 70 percent alcohol, which would be harmful in a mouth.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Mascara: Mascara is for lashes, and Maybelline's cake mascara of the 1910s was named for Mabel, the founder's sister.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Shampoo: The word comes from the Hindi 'champo', meaning to massage, and it is meant for hair, not teeth.
Things for cleaning your teeth.Sunscreen: SPF 30 blocks about 97 percent of UVB rays, which is useful on skin and useless on teeth.

Departments in a typical company.Human Resources: The term human resources came into wide use from the 1960s to the 1980s, replacing the older personnel department.
Departments in a typical company.Finance: Finance teams track cash and budgets, and the word comes from Old French 'finer', meaning to settle a debt.
Departments in a typical company.Marketing: Marketing means getting products in front of the right customers, and its famous 'four Ps' framework was popularised in 1960.
Departments in a typical company.Sales: Sales teams bring in revenue and are often paid commission on top of salary to reward closing deals.
Departments in a typical company.IT: IT stands for information technology, a term popularised in the 1950s, and staff keep computers, networks and passwords running.
Departments in a typical company.Legal: A legal department reviews contracts and handles disputes, and its in-house lawyers are often headed by a general counsel.
Departments in a typical company.Operations: Operations runs the day-to-day work of delivering a product or service, and the senior leader is often the chief operating officer.
Departments in a typical company.Customer service: Customer service handles complaints and questions, and a well-handled complaint often builds more loyalty than none at all.
Departments in a typical company.Procurement: Procurement buys the goods and services a company needs, negotiating prices and contracts with suppliers.
Departments in a typical company.Accounting: Double-entry bookkeeping, still the basis of accounting, was described by Luca Pacioli in 1494.
Departments in a typical company.Research: R&D at Bell Labs produced the transistor in 1947, a good example of what a research department can deliver.
Departments in a typical company.Payroll: Payroll makes sure everyone gets paid on time, calculating tax and deductions from a list once called the payroll.
Departments in a typical company.Recess: Recess is a school break for play, whereas companies have coffee breaks instead, though some tech firms have game rooms.
Departments in a typical company.Detention: Detention is a school punishment of staying after class; workplaces use warnings from HR instead.
Departments in a typical company.Homeroom: A homeroom is a class's base room where attendance is taken; offices just give you a desk.
Departments in a typical company.Playground: Playgrounds are school and park spaces; adults at work rarely use them, though some firms install them for staff.
Departments in a typical company.Cafeteria line: A cafeteria line is a school thing, though large firms also have canteens; it's not a department.
Departments in a typical company.Lost and found: Lost and found is a school office as well as a transport and hotel one; in companies reception usually handles it.
Departments in a typical company.Kindergarten: Kindergarten means 'children's garden' in German, a name coined by Friedrich Froebel in 1837.
Departments in a typical company.Nap time: Nap time is a preschool routine; some companies have napping pods but not a nap department.
Departments in a typical company.Show and tell: Show and tell has kids present objects to the class, whereas companies call it a presentation.
Departments in a typical company.Gym class: Gym class is school PE; firms may offer gym memberships but not a department called that.
Departments in a typical company.Story time: Story time is a library and preschool activity, not a department, though some firms hire storytellers for branding.
Departments in a typical company.Snack time: Snack time is for young kids, but offices stock snack cupboards, usually managed by facilities or an office manager.

Things sold in a hardware store.Nails: Nail sizes use 'penny' numbers, like 8d, from an old pricing system; the d stands for the Roman denarius.
Things sold in a hardware store.Screws: The Phillips head, developed in the 1930s, was designed so a driver cams out before it overtightens on assembly lines.
Things sold in a hardware store.Paint: Most hardware stores tint white base paint with pigments on demand, turning one can into thousands of colours.
Things sold in a hardware store.Hinges: Door hinges have existed for thousands of years, and the humble butt hinge still works on the same principle.
Things sold in a hardware store.Duct tape: Created in WWII to seal ammunition cases against water, it was first called duck tape for its cotton duck backing.
Things sold in a hardware store.Light bulbs: The Centennial Light in a California fire station has glowed almost continuously since 1901.
Things sold in a hardware store.Sandpaper: Despite the name it rarely uses sand; aluminium oxide or silicon carbide grit does the work, and higher numbers mean finer paper.
Things sold in a hardware store.Extension cord: Thin cords can overheat if overloaded, which is why they carry a maximum amp or watt rating.
Things sold in a hardware store.Padlocks: Many padlocks use pin tumblers, a design from ancient Egypt that Linus Yale Jr. refined in the 1860s.
Things sold in a hardware store.Hammers: The claw for pulling nails dates to Roman times, and the oldest stone hammers are millions of years old.
Things sold in a hardware store.Wood glue: A properly cured wood joint can be stronger than the wood itself, which often breaks before the glue does.
Things sold in a hardware store.Drill bits: The twist drill bit was invented by Stephen Morse in 1861; its spiral flutes clear shavings from the hole.
Things sold in a hardware store.Stethoscopes: A medical supply item, though hardware stores do sell a mechanic's stethoscope for finding engine noises, so it's a close call.
Things sold in a hardware store.Lettuce: Groceries sell it; ancient Egyptians grew lettuce and considered it sacred to the fertility god Min.
Things sold in a hardware store.Lipstick: It goes back thousands of years to Mesopotamia, long before the swivel tube of 1915.
Things sold in a hardware store.Fresh fish: A fishmonger's product; the nearest a hardware store comes is some of the tackle for catching it.
Things sold in a hardware store.Wedding dresses: Queen Victoria's white gown in 1840 made white the fashionable colour for brides.
Things sold in a hardware store.Library books: Libraries lend them rather than sell them; Benjamin Franklin helped found a lending library in Philadelphia in 1731.
Things sold in a hardware store.Concert tickets: Sold by venues and online agents, not hardware stores; many are now just a QR code on a phone.
Things sold in a hardware store.Prescription drugs: A pharmacist dispenses them on prescription; the symbol Rx comes from the Latin recipe, meaning take.
Things sold in a hardware store.Sushi: The word refers to the sour-tasting vinegared rice, not the fish, and it isn't sold beside the hammers.
Things sold in a hardware store.Perfume: The word is often traced to Latin per fumum, meaning through smoke, from burning incense.
Things sold in a hardware store.Ball gowns: The crinolines of the 1850s made skirts so wide that doorways became a real challenge.
Things sold in a hardware store.Puppies: A pet shop or breeder sells them; puppies sleep about 18 to 20 hours a day while growing.

Things a florist sells.Roses: Fossils show roses are about 35 million years old, and colors like blue don't exist naturally, so blue roses are dyed.
Things a florist sells.Tulips: In 1630s Holland, a single rare tulip bulb sometimes cost more than a house, in a speculation craze called tulip mania.
Things a florist sells.Lilies: Lilies are poisonous to cats, and even pollen or vase water can cause serious kidney trouble for them.
Things a florist sells.Carnations: Carnations are among the oldest cultivated flowers, around 2,000 years, and they are a classic for Mother's Day.
Things a florist sells.Orchids: Orchids are among the biggest plant families, with some 25,000 species, and vanilla comes from one.
Things a florist sells.Daisies: The name comes from "day's eye", because the flower closes at night and opens with the sun.
Things a florist sells.Bouquets: The word is French for a little wood, and Victorian bouquets, called tussie-mussies, used flowers to send coded messages.
Things a florist sells.Wreaths: Ancient Greeks crowned winners with wreaths of laurel, and today they hang as door decorations and at funerals.
Things a florist sells.Sunflowers: Young sunflowers follow the sun across the sky in a way called heliotropism, but mature blooms generally face east.
Things a florist sells.Peonies: Peonies can live for decades, and are prized in China, where they were long considered the king of flowers.
Things a florist sells.Corsages: A small flower worn on a dress or wrist, the corsage became a prom and wedding tradition, from the French for bodice.
Things a florist sells.Lettuce: It's a vegetable, and grows from seed to harvest in just a couple of months, but a florist doesn't stock it.
Things a florist sells.Carrots: Carrot flowers are lacy, and the wild carrot is also called Queen Anne's lace, but the root belongs to the greengrocer.
Things a florist sells.Mushrooms: Mushrooms are fungi, not plants, which is one more reason they don't belong with the flowers.
Things a florist sells.Seaweed: It is algae, not a flower, and it is used in sushi and even in ice cream as a thickener.
Things a florist sells.Potatoes: Potato plants do flower, but the harvest is the underground tuber, which a greengrocer sells.
Things a florist sells.Onions: Onions are related to lilies, and the flower is a ball of tiny stars, though no florist sells them for eating.
Things a florist sells.Garlic: Garlic belongs to the same family as lilies, and was fed to the builders of the Egyptian pyramids, according to ancient accounts.
Things a florist sells.Cabbage: Ornamental cabbages and kale are sold in autumn as pretty garden plants, but eating one from a florist isn't the plan.
Things a florist sells.Celery: Celery was once grown for medicine, and its wild form is called smallage, long before it was salad.
Things a florist sells.Leeks: A leek is a leaf-and-stem vegetable, and its flower, if left to grow, is a big purple ball.
Things a florist sells.Parsnips: Before sugar was common, parsnips were used as a sweetener in Europe, and a greengrocer sells them.
Things a florist sells.Radishes: Radishes can be ready in about three weeks, making them one of the fastest crops from seed to table.
Things a florist sells.Turnips: Before pumpkins, people in Ireland and Scotland carved turnips for Halloween lanterns.

Consoles whose games came on cartridges.Xbox: The original Xbox used DVDs and had a built-in hard drive.

Consoles whose games came on cartridges.GameCube: The GameCube used small proprietary mini discs rather than cartridges.
Consoles whose games came on cartridges.Wii: The Wii used discs, though its sleek drive also played GameCube games.
Consoles whose games came on cartridges.Xbox 360: The Xbox 360 used DVDs, with later titles needing multiple discs.
Consoles whose games came on cartridges.PS3: The PS3 used Blu-ray discs, which gave games much more space.

Cities in Silicon Valley.Menlo Park: Meta (Facebook) headquarters stands here, a small city where Facebook moved in 2011.
Cities in Silicon Valley.Sunnyvale: Atari was founded here in 1972, and Yahoo and LinkedIn long had offices.
Cities in Silicon Valley.Santa Clara: Intel's headquarters is here, as is Levi's Stadium, home of the 49ers.

Cities in Silicon Valley.Redwood City: Electronic Arts is based here, and the city's slogan is Climate Best By Government Test.
Cities in Silicon Valley.Los Gatos: Netflix is headquartered in this foothill town, whose name means the cats in Spanish.
Cities in Silicon Valley.Milpitas: At the valley's northeast end, it hosts chip equipment firms, including KLA.
Cities in Silicon Valley.Los Altos: Steve Jobs's family home here, with its garage, is often cited as the Apple's early workspace.
Cities in Silicon Valley.Campbell: Once part of the fruit-growing Valley of Heart's Delight, filled with orchards before tech.
Cities in Silicon Valley.Seattle: A Pacific Northwest tech hub, home to Amazon and Microsoft's region, but far from Silicon Valley.
Cities in Silicon Valley.Austin: A Texas tech city, nicknamed Silicon Hills, not Silicon Valley.
Cities in Silicon Valley.Boston: Home to MIT and Route 128, a rival tech corridor in Massachusetts.
Cities in Silicon Valley.Los Angeles: Known for entertainment, with a tech scene dubbed Silicon Beach, not Silicon Valley.

Art museums.Louvre: The world's most visited museum is a former royal palace in Paris, home to the Mona Lisa and the Venus de Milo.
Art museums.Uffizi: Florence's gallery was built in the 1560s as offices for the Medici, hence the name, which means "offices" in Italian.
Art museums.Prado: Madrid's museum holds Velázquez's Las Meninas and Goya's disturbing Black Paintings.
Art museums.Rijksmuseum: Amsterdam's national museum holds Rembrandt's Night Watch, and a public bike path runs straight through its ground floor.
Art museums.Tate Modern: London's gallery of modern art is housed in a former power station on the Thames, with a vast turbine hall.
Art museums.MoMA: New York's museum of modern art opened in 1929, just days after the stock market crash, and owns Van Gogh's Starry Night.
Art museums.Guggenheim: Frank Lloyd Wright's spiral building in New York opened in 1959; its sister in Bilbao, by Frank Gehry, opened in 1997.
Art museums.Hermitage: This Saint Petersburg museum was started by Catherine the Great in 1764, and cats still guard its cellars from mice.
Art museums.Musée d'Orsay: A former railway station on the Seine now shows the world's largest Impressionist collection under its big station clock.
Art museums.National Gallery: London's gallery on Trafalgar Square is free to enter and holds Van Gogh's Sunflowers.
Art museums.Getty Center: This hilltop Los Angeles complex, opened in 1997, is clad in travertine stone and holds art, gardens and views.
Art museums.The Met: New York's Metropolitan Museum was founded in 1870 and houses a complete Egyptian temple, the Temple of Dendur.
Art museums.Van Gogh Museum: Amsterdam's museum holds the world's biggest Van Gogh collection, including over 200 of his paintings.
Art museums.Bodleian Library: Oxford's library is a copyright library with millions of books, one of Europe's oldest, a place for reading not for paintings.
Art museums.Colosseum: Rome's amphitheater held about 50,000 spectators for gladiator fights; it's an ancient arena, not an art gallery.
Art museums.Parthenon: Athens' temple to Athena once displayed a giant gold-and-ivory statue; it's architecture, not an art museum.
Art museums.Carnegie Hall: New York's concert hall opened in 1891 with Tchaikovsky conducting; it's for music, not paintings.
Art museums.La Scala: Milan's opera house is a famed stage, not a museum, though it does have a small museum attached.
Art museums.Bolshoi Theatre: Moscow's theatre has hosted ballet and opera since 1825; its name means "big".
Art museums.Globe Theatre: Shakespeare's playhouse, rebuilt near its original site in 1997, is a theatre rather than an art museum.
Art museums.Sydney Opera House: Jørn Utzon's sail-roofed building is a performing arts center, not a gallery.
Art museums.Royal Albert Hall: London's concert hall seats over 5,000 and hosts the Proms each summer.
Art museums.Wembley Stadium: England's national stadium, with its arch about 130 metres tall, is for football.
Art museums.Lincoln Center: New York's performing arts center is home to the Met Opera and New York City Ballet.

Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Apple: Much of an apple's fiber and many antioxidants are in its peel, so peeling it removes a lot of nutrition.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Grape: Grape skin holds the pigments and compounds like resveratrol, and it gives red wine its color.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Pear: Pear skin has much of the fruit's fiber, and it can taste slightly gritty from tiny stone cells.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Peach: A peach's fuzz is made of tiny hairs; its smooth cousin, the nectarine, is the same species.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Plum: Plum skin is slightly tart, and the whitish bloom on it is a natural wax you can wipe off.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Cherry: Cherries are eaten whole except for the pit, and the skin gives tart cherries their rich color.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Blueberry: The blue of a blueberry comes from the waxy bloom on its skin, and the pigments are anthocyanins.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Strawberry: The tiny seeds on a strawberry's skin are each a separate fruit, and strawberries are not true berries.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Fig: Fig skin is edible, and the fruit is actually an inverted flower, with a hollow stem holding hundreds of tiny blossoms.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Apricot: Apricot skin is thin and velvety, and the fruit is eaten whole except for the stone.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Tomato: Tomato skin is eaten raw but often peeled for sauces, and the fruit is a botanical berry.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Nectarine: A nectarine is a peach variety with a gene for smooth skin, and no fuzz is needed.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Banana: Banana peel is edible in some cuisines when cooked, but most people discard it, and it is bitter.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Orange: Orange peel is edible and holds fragrant oils used in zest and marmalade, but the pith is bitter.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Pineapple: A pineapple's skin is spiky and tough, and the fruit is made of many fused berries.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Watermelon: Watermelon rind is edible and is pickled in the American South and in Chinese cooking.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Avocado: Avocado skin is bitter and contains persin, so people peel it.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Coconut: A coconut has a fibrous husk and hard shell, which are unedible, though the husk is used in rope and mats.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Pomegranate: A pomegranate's leathery rind is bitter, and the edible parts are the seeds, called arils.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Lychee: Lychee has a rough shell that's discarded, and the seed inside is mildly toxic.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Grapefruit: Grapefruit has a thick bitter peel, and it is a cross between a pomelo and an orange.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Cantaloupe: Cantaloupe's netted rind is tough and can harbor bacteria, so it is typically peeled and washed.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Passion fruit: Passion fruit has a tough rind you discard, and the pulp inside is eaten with its seeds.
Fruits whose skin you usually eat.Dragon fruit: Dragon fruit has leathery scales, and the skin is typically discarded, since it's bitter.

Colors named after gemstones.Emerald: Emerald green is named for the gem, a variety of beryl whose color comes from traces of chromium.
Colors named after gemstones.Ruby: Ruby red is named after the gem, and rubies are one of the hardest minerals after diamonds.
Colors named after gemstones.Sapphire: Sapphire blue comes from the gem, which in fact occurs in nearly every color except red.
Colors named after gemstones.Amethyst: Amethyst's name comes from Greek meaning 'not intoxicated', as ancients believed it prevented drunkenness.
Colors named after gemstones.Turquoise: Turquoise is named from French for 'Turkish', since the stone reached Europe through Turkey.
Colors named after gemstones.Jade: Jade is green in name, but the gem comes in various colors, and ancient China valued it above gold.
Colors named after gemstones.Topaz: Topaz can be colorless, though the color named topaz is a golden yellow or orange.
Colors named after gemstones.Amber: Amber is fossilized tree resin rather than a true mineral, and it sometimes preserves ancient insects.
Colors named after gemstones.Onyx: Onyx is a banded stone, and the color onyx is a deep black.
Colors named after gemstones.Garnet: Garnet's name comes from a word for pomegranate, because its red crystals resemble the fruit's seeds.
Colors named after gemstones.Aquamarine: Aquamarine means 'seawater' in Latin, and sailors carried it as a charm for safe voyages.
Colors named after gemstones.Lavender: Lavender is named for a plant, and its purple flowers have been used in perfume and sleep aids.
Colors named after gemstones.Salmon: Salmon is named after the fish, whose pink-orange flesh comes from its diet of crustaceans.
Colors named after gemstones.Olive: Olive is named after the fruit of the olive tree, and unripe olives are green.
Colors named after gemstones.Mustard: Mustard yellow gets its name from the condiment, which is made from ground mustard seeds.
Colors named after gemstones.Peach: Peach is a color named after the fruit, and the fruit is native to China.
Colors named after gemstones.Navy: Navy blue is named for the dark uniforms of the British Royal Navy.
Colors named after gemstones.Lime: Lime green is named after the citrus fruit, and limes were once given to sailors to prevent scurvy.
Colors named after gemstones.Chocolate: Chocolate brown is named for the food, and the color is a deep brown.
Colors named after gemstones.Cherry: Cherry red is named after the fruit, and a cherry-colored car is a classic.
Colors named after gemstones.Mint: Mint green is named for the leafy herb, and menthol is what creates the cool sensation.
Colors named after gemstones.Teal: Teal is named for a small duck whose head has a blue-green stripe.
Colors named after gemstones.Magenta: Magenta is named after a battle fought in 1859 in Italy, around the time the dye was discovered.
Colors named after gemstones.Charcoal: Charcoal is a dark gray named for burnt wood, which has been used for drawing and fuel.

Flowers known for a sweet scent.Jasmine: Jasmine blooms release most scent at night, and the flowers are picked before dawn for perfume.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Lavender: Lavender's scent comes from linalool and linalyl acetate, and it's used in sachets to repel moths.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Gardenia: Gardenia has an intense creamy fragrance, and Coco Chanel's perfume line featured one in a signature scent.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Lilac: Lilacs bloom for only a couple of weeks in spring, and their scent is one of the best known in garden flowers.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Honeysuckle: Honeysuckle flowers have sweet nectar that children have sipped for generations, though the berries are poisonous.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Freesia: Freesia is named after a German doctor, and its citrusy scent makes it a popular choice for bouquets and perfumes.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Hyacinth: A single hyacinth bulb can perfume a whole room, and the flower is named for a figure from Greek myth.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Sweet pea: Sweet peas are scented climbing flowers, but their seeds are poisonous, unlike garden peas.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Plumeria: Plumeria is used in Hawaiian leis, and its fragrance is strongest in the evening to attract moths.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Orange blossom: Orange blossom water has flavored Middle Eastern sweets for centuries, and the flowers are a traditional wedding symbol.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Tuberose: Tuberose has a heavy, intoxicating scent and is among the priciest perfume flowers, and it's strongest at night.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Sunflower: Sunflowers have a mild scent at best, but their heads track the sun when young.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Dahlia: Dahlias are the national flower of Mexico, and they have little fragrance despite their spectacular blooms.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Gerbera daisy: Gerbera daisies come in bright colors and have almost no scent, and they're related to sunflowers.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Begonia: Begonias are grown for colorful blooms and foliage, and most have little scent.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Poinsettia: The red parts of a poinsettia are leaves, not petals, and it has no notable fragrance.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Bird of paradise: This flower looks like a tropical bird's head and has little scent, and it's the official flower of Los Angeles.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Anthurium: Anthuriums have glossy, heart-shaped flower bracts and almost no scent, and they last for weeks.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Zinnia: Zinnias are cheerful and bright, and have little scent, but they were the first flowers grown on the space station.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Corpse flower: The corpse flower is famous for smelling like rotting flesh, which attracts the flies that pollinate it.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Hydrangea: Hydrangea blooms change color from pink to blue depending on how acidic the soil is, and they have little scent.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Camellia: Camellias are beautiful, but most have barely any scent, and tea comes from a camellia species.
Flowers known for a sweet scent.Impatiens: Impatiens are named for their seed pods, which burst open at a touch, and they have no scent.

American vehicle brands.Chrysler: Chrysler was founded by Walter Chrysler in 1925, and his Chrysler Building in New York was briefly the tallest in the world.
American vehicle brands.Lincoln: Lincoln is Ford's luxury brand, named for Abraham Lincoln, and its cars have been used by US presidents.
American vehicle brands.GMC: GMC makes trucks and SUVs, and it stands for General Motors Truck Company, which dates back to 1912.
American vehicle brands.Rivian: Rivian is an American electric truck and SUV maker founded in 2009, and Amazon is a big customer for its delivery vans.

American vehicle brands.Harley-Davidson: Harley-Davidson was founded in Milwaukee in 1903 by William Harley and Arthur Davidson, in a tiny wooden shed.

American vehicle brands.Lexus: Lexus is Japanese, not American; Toyota launched it in 1989 as its luxury brand, mainly aimed at the US market.
American vehicle brands.Peugeot: Peugeot is French and one of the oldest car brands, with a family firm that dates to 1810, and it isn't American.

Nautical terms.Port: Port replaced the old 'larboard' for the ship's left side because larboard sounded too much like starboard.
Nautical terms.Starboard: Starboard comes from 'steerboard', since early ships were steered with a side-mounted oar on the right.
Nautical terms.Bow: The bow is the front of a ship, and the bowline knot got its name from that.
Nautical terms.Stern: The stern is the back of a ship, and old sterns carried ornate captain's cabins and carved galleries.
Nautical terms.Hull: Royal Navy ships had their hulls sheathed in copper from the 1760s to stop shipworm and barnacles.
Nautical terms.Keel: The keel is a ship's backbone, which is where we get 'keel over' and 'on an even keel'.
Nautical terms.Bilge: The bilge is the lowest part of a ship's hull where dirty water gathers, and 'bilge' also means nonsense.
Nautical terms.Knot: A knot is one nautical mile per hour, and the name comes from knotted rope thrown overboard to measure speed.
Nautical terms.Leeward: Leeward is the side away from the wind, so it is sheltered, and the Leeward Islands are named for it.
Nautical terms.Windward: Windward is the side facing the wind, and the Windward Islands face the trade winds.
Nautical terms.Fathom: A fathom is six feet, about 1.8 metres, from an Old English word for outstretched arms.
Nautical terms.Pantograph: A pantograph is the arm that draws power from overhead wires on electric trains, so it belongs to railways.
Nautical terms.Caboose: A caboose was the crew car at the end of a freight train, not a ship's part.
Nautical terms.Fuselage: The fuselage is the main body of an airplane, so it is aviation, not nautical.
Nautical terms.Aileron: An aileron is a wing flap on an airplane, so it belongs to aviation.
Nautical terms.Taxiway: A taxiway is the path planes follow at airports, so it isn't nautical.
Nautical terms.Odometer: The odometer counts a vehicle's mileage, and a ship uses a log to measure distance.
Nautical terms.Kickstand: A kickstand props up a bicycle or motorbike, and a ship has no use for one.
Nautical terms.Hubcap: A hubcap covers a wheel's center, so ships have none.
Nautical terms.Sleeper: A sleeper is a railway beam, or a bed on a night train, not a ship part.
Nautical terms.Clutch: A clutch connects an engine to the gearbox in a car, and it is not a ship's equipment.
Nautical terms.Siding: A siding is a short railway track, so it isn't a ship part.
Nautical terms.Spoiler: A spoiler is a car or airplane wing-shaped part, and it isn't found on boats.
Nautical terms.Turnstile: A turnstile is a rotating gate at stations and stadiums, and it is not a ship part.

Fictional rabbits.Lola Bunny: Lola Bunny joined Bugs in Space Jam in 1996, as a basketball star.
Fictional rabbits.Miffy: Miffy is a Dutch rabbit created by Dick Bruna in 1955, drawn with simple bold lines.
Fictional rabbits.Bunnicula: Bunnicula is a vampire rabbit, a children's novel by the Howes, 1979, and he sucks juice from vegetables.
Fictional rabbits.Velveteen Rabbit: The Velveteen Rabbit is a toy who becomes real through being loved, a classic from 1922.
Fictional rabbits.Easter Bunny: The Easter Bunny came to the US with German immigrants, and the hare laid colored eggs for good children.

Fictional rabbits.Bambi: Bambi is a deer, not a rabbit; he is the young prince of the forest, and Thumper is the rabbit who befriends him.

Star Trek species.Klingon: Warriors with forehead ridges who revere honour in battle; their language was invented for Star Trek III.
Star Trek species.Vulcan: Spock's half-human heritage makes him an outsider; Vulcans nearly destroyed themselves with emotion before embracing logic.
Star Trek species.Romulan: Descended from Vulcans who rejected logic, Romulans hid behind a Neutral Zone and cloaking tech.
Star Trek species.Borg: Assimilating others with nanoprobes, the Borg were introduced in The Next Generation's second season, and Locutus was Picard's assimilated self.
Star Trek species.Ferengi: Obsessed with profit and with big ears, Ferengi were meant as villains but became comic relief, especially Quark in Deep Space Nine.
Star Trek species.Cardassian: Ridged-necked occupiers of Bajor, who feature largely in Deep Space Nine; Gul Dukat and Garak are notable ones.
Star Trek species.Bajoran: Spiritual people with nose ridges whose planet was occupied; Kira Nerys served on Deep Space Nine.
Star Trek species.Andorian: Blue-skinned with antennae, Andorians were founding Federation members, seen in Star Trek: Enterprise as well.
Star Trek species.Tribble: Fluffy, purring and born pregnant, they multiplied wildly in the 1967 episode, and Kirk was buried in them.
Star Trek species.Gorn: Reptilian foe whom Captain Kirk fought on a rocky planet in 1967, with a famously goofy rubber suit.
Star Trek species.Betazoid: Telepaths such as Counselor Deanna Troi, who is half Betazoid and half human, can sense emotions.
Star Trek species.Wookiee: Chewbacca's species is from Star Wars, not Trek, and they're known for ripping arms off sore losers.
Star Trek species.Ewok: The small furry Endor tribe is Star Wars through and through.
Star Trek species.Jawa: Tatooine's hooded scrap traders belong to Star Wars, not Star Trek.
Star Trek species.Dalek: Doctor Who's mutant cyborg tanks, not from the Federation; their name was coined by writer Terry Nation.
Star Trek species.Cyberman: Doctor Who's silver cyborg, a Trek-style foe on the surface, but from the Whoniverse.
Star Trek species.Na'vi: The blue natives of Pandora from James Cameron's Avatar, with no Starfleet connection.
Star Trek species.Kree: Marvel alien warriors, in Guardians of the Galaxy and Captain Marvel, not a Trek species.
Star Trek species.Skrull: Marvel's green shapeshifters, who sneak into human society, are not from Star Trek.
Star Trek species.Time Lord: Doctor Who's long-lived race from Gallifrey, with regeneration, not found in Trek.
Star Trek species.Hutt: Star Wars crime-lord slugs like Jabba, not from Star Trek.
Star Trek species.Gungan: Naboo's amphibious residents like Jar Jar Binks belong to Star Wars.
Star Trek species.Sontaran: Doctor Who's short, clone-bred warrior race, who have a probic vent at the back of their necks, are not from Trek.
Star Trek species.Kryptonian: Superman's people from the planet Krypton, which belong to DC comics, not Star Trek.

Things from Star Wars.Death Star: The first Death Star is about 120 km across; Rebels exploit a tiny exhaust port left unshielded.
Things from Star Wars.TIE fighter: Its screech was made from an elephant's call mixed with a car passing on wet pavement; TIE stands for Twin Ion Engine.
Things from Star Wars.The Force: An energy field that ties all living things together, which Obi-Wan describes as binding the galaxy; midi-chlorians were later added to explain it.
Things from Star Wars.Jedi: An order of Force-sensitive peacekeepers, whose name partly echoes the Japanese jidaigeki, period dramas.
Things from Star Wars.Sith: Dark-side Force users who follow a rule of two: a master and an apprentice, since the days of Darth Bane.
Things from Star Wars.Blaster: Star Wars' energy pistol, famously wielded by Han Solo, a DL-44 heavy blaster.
Things from Star Wars.Stormtrooper: Imperial soldiers famed for terrible aim; the original clone troopers were all modeled on Jango Fett.
Things from Star Wars.Carbonite: The freezing process used to preserve Han Solo for Jabba, which he survives with hibernation sickness.
Things from Star Wars.Holocron: A Jedi or Sith data cube containing ancient knowledge, opened only by those with the Force.
Things from Star Wars.Kyber crystal: The rare crystal that powers lightsabers and the Death Star's superlaser, and its colour depends on its owner.
Things from Star Wars.Bacta tank: A liquid-filled healing tank, where Luke recovers after the wampa attack and Wampa's claws on Hoth.
Things from Star Wars.Phaser: Star Trek's handheld energy weapon, with stun settings, is not from Star Wars.
Things from Star Wars.Tricorder: Star Trek's handheld scanner, used by Spock, doesn't appear in a galaxy far away.
Things from Star Wars.Warp drive: Star Trek's method for faster-than-light travel; Star Wars uses hyperdrive.
Things from Star Wars.TARDIS: Doctor Who's time machine ship, which looks like a police box.
Things from Star Wars.Starfleet: The Federation's space exploration force in Star Trek, not the Rebel Alliance.
Things from Star Wars.Transporter: Star Trek's matter-beaming device, a budget-saving idea because shuttlecraft landings were too expensive to film.
Things from Star Wars.Sonic screwdriver: Doctor Who's gadget, which doesn't fit the Star Wars universe.
Things from Star Wars.Holodeck: Star Trek's simulated-reality room, absent from Star Wars.
Things from Star Wars.Dilithium: Star Trek's crystal that regulates warp drive, unlike Star Wars's kyber crystals.
Things from Star Wars.Prime Directive: Starfleet's rule against interfering with other cultures, not part of Star Wars.
Things from Star Wars.Flux capacitor: Back to the Future's time-travel part, in a different movie universe.
Things from Star Wars.Proton pack: The Ghostbusters' unlicensed nuclear accelerator, not a Star Wars thing.
